speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of Finance) moved
subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 (NO. 3) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
that Bill C-143, to provide supplementary borrowing authority, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, upon my appointment as Minister of Finance I said that one of my basic tenets would be fully to inform the Canadian people fully of the economic situation as I saw it. I have done this repeatedly and consistently since my appointment as Minister of Finance, and I will continue to do this today and in the future Not only is it a right for the Canadian people to know of the economic situation in the country, but I also believe it is essential for the confidence and solidarity that will ensure economic recovery.
I am pleased to open debate on the borrowing authority Bill which is before us today. This Bill is one in a series of necessary steps being taken to deal with the extremely difficult economic situation facing this country. The Bill is a reflection of the massive financial support that the Government of Canada is providing to the economy and particularly to the victims of the recession. It reflects the severity of the recession itself.
The need for a borrowing Bill before the end of this fiscal year on April 1 was spelled out in my economic statement of October 27. At that time, the Government reaffirmed its commitment to help those who need it the most through the Unemployment Insurance Program, the Canada Assistance Plan and a number of other initiatives such as direct job creation.
This help was given at the very time when revenues were falling rapidly because of the recession. The inevitable effect of this humane and vital provision of economic support is an increase in the deficit and in the borrowing requirements of the Government. I laid it all out in October and I appreciated the wide support for this approach from Members of the House and individuals and groups all across Canada.
In fact, the need for this Bill at this time was one of the few sure things on which we could depend in an inherently volatile economic situation. If any Hon. Member is surprised by this Bill, then he or she was not paying attention to the real world outside.
After I assumed the Finance portfolio almost five months ago, I was asked how long I would need to settle into the job. My reply was to the effect that I was not sure how much time I would need, but I already knew how much time was available; that is, virtually none. Looking back, I now realize how fortunate I was not to have had a lot of time to settle in. The economic and financial ground on which we were treading had all the less desirable qualities of quicksand. The last thing any of us would have wanted to do, indeed, would be to settle in.
Clearly, the economic situation is starting to show more positive developments. There are more and more signs of an emerging recovery. However, it would be premature to say today that the economic and financial footing has completely stabilized. The risks remain high, but they will diminish considerably if we all work together in a determined effort to pull this country through. We in this House should be vigorously supporting the emerging new economic momentum, and that means getting on with the business at hand.
The Bill is just one in a series of important steps following the October statement. Another major step was the introduction of the income tax legislation which would provide certainty by clearing up unresolved tax issues dating back to November, 1981, and which includes adjustments announced in my October statement.

In my October statement to Parliament, I indicated that the real Gross National Product was expected to fall by 4.4 per cent in 1982, and that unemployment was expected to decline very slowly through 1983.

speechtext:
Most of the private sector forecasts which i have recently seen have projected real GNP growth for 1983 to be in the 1 per cent to 2 per cent range. I plan to outline the Government's own projections for 1983 and the years beyond in my forthcoming budget speech.
As I have already indicated, the delay in the economic recovery has had the effect of further reducing federal revenues and increasing financial requirements. Under the Financial Administration Act, statutory borrowing authority must be obtained from Parliament in order for the Government to increase its outstanding debt. The Bill currently before the House seeks new borrowing authority of $19 billion. This amount is made up of $5 billion supplementary borrowing authority for 1982-83 and $14 billion interim borrowing authority for 1983-84.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 (NO. 3) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: Why?

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 (NO. 3) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
As Hon. Members will recall, so far this fiscal year the Government has obtained borrowing authority amounting to $21.1 billion. This amount is made up of $3.5 billion of unused borrowing authority carried forward from earlier years; $6.6 billion for 1982-83 provided by Bill C-111; $7 billion provided by Bill C-125 and a further $4 billion provided by Bill C-128.
As a matter of interest to Hon. Members, I would like to set out the Government's debt program so far in the current fiscal year and the amount of borrowing authority that has been used to date. To February 1 1, 1983, a total of $20.6 billion of borrowing authority had been used of the $21.1 billion authorized. The use of borrowing authority is made up of $0.9 billion as a result of foreign borrowing and about $19.7 billion as a result of the domestic debt program. The main component of the foreign borrowing was the borrowing of $750 million U.S. in the Eurobond market last June. The domestic debt program comprised approximately $7.1 billion raised through the net issue of treasury bills; $4.5 billion through the net issue of marketable bonds; and after taking the net redemptions into account, $8.1 billion through Canada Savings Bonds.
Hon. Members will note that the amount of borrowing power already obtained for 1982-83 is smaller than the $22.2 billion financial requirements forecast last October in my statement in this House. The latest projections now forecast financial requirements at $26.1 billion for 1982-83. The upward revision of $3.9 billion of financial requirements since
February 17, 1983

October reflects a downward adjustment of S2.5 billion to the revenue forecast, an upward revision of $1.2 billion to projected total outlays and a $0.2 billion change to estimated annual budgetary transactions.
The projected budgetary deficit for the current fiscal year rises to $27.2 billion, up from $23.6 billion since the October statement. The increase in the deficit is slightly less than the increase for financial requirements because of the non-budgetary component of the latter which I have mentioned.
From the press reports of the past two days, it appears that some have been confusing the financial requirements of the Government with the Government's deficit. This is somewhat surprising since over the years the two numbers have not been identical. As I just mentioned, the figures as of October 27 were $22.2 billion for financial requirements and $23.6 billion for the deficit. The deficit, of course, reflects the same economic pressures that have increased our financial requirements since October. It equally reflects the Government's commitment to ease the impact of the recession on individual Canadians and the economy as a whole.
Revenues from the corporate income tax, the personal income tax and the petroleum and gas revenue tax have all been falling short of previously anticipated levels. The increase in total outlays is primarily the result of non-discretionary cost increases for statutory programs, most notably public debt charges, Government contributions to Unemployment Insurance extended benefits, equalization, Established Programs Financing and veterans' pensions.
It also includes a $240 million adjustment to cover anticipated additional requirements under the Canadian Home Ownership Stimulation Program. As of January, 1983 a total of 158,900 grants worth $476 million had been issued under this program, which obviously has been a great success. Finally, non-budgetary transactions are now expected to provide a somewhat smaller net source of funds than forecast earlier because of further widening in the Unemployment Insurance account deficit.
In summary, about 72 per cent of the increase in the estimated financial requirements for 1982-83 since the updated projections in October, 1982 reflects revenue losses and higher than expected debt charges as a result of the delay in the start of the economic recovery. Another 28 per cent consists of a variety of recession-related expenditures such as those required under established income support programs. Increases in Unemployment Insurance payments account for almost one-third of these expenditures.
In light of the estimated financial requirements for 1982-83 which I have just outlined, Part I of this Bill requests additional borrowing authority for this fiscal year of $5 billion. This amount of borrowing authority, in addition to the amounts already available for this Fiscal year, will result in total authorized borrowing authority equal to the financial requirements for 1982-83.
Members will note that in Part I of this Bill, as in Bill C-125 and other previous borrowing authority Bills, some portion of
Borrowing Authority
the authority is to be non-lapsing. In the case of the present Bill, the non-lapsing amount will be $2 billion. The need for the non-lapsing authority rises from the uncertainty of the date of the passage of this Bill and the desire to tailor the Government's borrowing operations to financial market conditions. Thus, it may be that some of this year's financial requirements will be temporarily met by a rundown in cash balances. Nonetheless, the financial requirements must ultimately be met by borrowing and the non-lapsing amount in the authority provides a basis for such borrowing after March 31 of this year.
Concerning fiscal year 1983-84, it is still too early to forecast what the total financial requirements will be. They will, of course, depend upon the measures to be included in the budget. They will also depend upon the course of economic developments through 1983 and 1984, and my officials and myself are still reviewing the economic outlook. The results of this review will be outlined in the budget which I will present to the House.
However, I would like to announce at this time that the Government has reviewed the expenditure framework for 1983-84, and for planning purposes has agreed on a total outlay target of $88.9 billion for 1983-84. This represents an increase of 9.6 per cent relative to total outlays in the current fiscal year.
The President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray) will be providing Parliament with detailed expenditure Estimates for 1983-84 on February 22, when he tables the Main Estimates, and I will be providing Parliament with full information on the Government's expenditure plan, including any changes the Government may make for the current fiscal year, at the time of my budget.
I intend to introduce a Bill covering all of the borrowing authority needed for fiscal year 1983-84 after providing Parliament with the necessary information in my budget. This Bill will also take into account the interim borrowing authority to be granted on the basis of the Bill now before the House.
It is desirable that Parliament have adequate time to study and debate the budget as well as the new borrowing authority. At the same time, it is necessary for the Government to carry out its debt program in an orderly, efficient manner, and this will require borrowing authority. Our request in Part II of the Bill for $14 billion borrowing authority for part of 1983-84 is based on both these considerations I have mentioned.
Financial requirements in 1983-84 will continue to be high. The amount of interim authority requested, however, is sufficient to last into the summer, and this will provide a stable basis for debt operation while Parliament is considering the budget and the related borrowing authority Bill. I might note that the first fiscal quarter is a period of particularly heavy seasonal cash requirements because of tax reforms which amount to roughly $6 billion and other factors. It is, therefore,

February 17, 1983
Borrowing Authority
of particular importance that borrowing operations not be hindered by borrowing authority constraints.

Let me now explain in more detail why passage of this bill and provision of interim borrowing authority for 1983-84 is important.
As members are probably aware, Government of Canada securities currently outstanding amount to more than $113 billion, and financial requirements are such that they will require that the outstanding debt increase by an average of about $2 billion every month. In addition, previously issued debt is coming due and must be re-financed. For example, something in the neighbourhood of $1.25 billion worth of Treasury bills must be re-financed each week and there are significant maturities in the bond market.
Clearly, given the size of the financial operations which I have just described, even a savings of a small fraction of one per cent can imply significant dollar amounts. Since the major objective of debt management is to minimize public debt charges it is important that the borrowing program can be planned and operated in an orderly and efficient manner and that the Government have the flexibility to respond to attractive financing opportunities. Clearly, adequate borrowing authority is necessary for this to be achieved.
Another important objective of debt management is compatibility with the smooth and efficient operation of the financial markets. Besides being cost-effective, this helps to ensure that federal borrowing operations do not interfere with borrowing activities by other levels of government or the private sector. Adequate borrowing authority is essential for the type of planning and flexible response to changing financial market conditions which ensure that the financial markets are not disrupted by government borrowing.
There is an additional need for ensuring adequate borrowing authority which has been mentioned in previous debates-that is the impact of exchange market operations. The estimated financial requirements which I have been discussing do not take into account any possible impact from exchange operations. When the Canadian dollar is firm, as it has been in recent months, exchange reserves will increase. To finance this increase, Canadian dollar must be borrowed and charged against the borrowing authority. On the other hand, in periods when the Canadian dollar is under heavy pressure and our U.S. dollar working balances are low, these U.S. dollar balances are supplemented by drawing on the standby credits which the government has with the Canadian and international banks.
Thus, if the government is to carry out its responsibilities under the Currency and Exchange Act in an efficient and cost-effective manner, borrowing authority must be in place to accommodate exchange market pressures.
To sum up, dealing with this bill in a business-like and responsible manner and providing adequate interim borrowing authority will benefit the taxpayer by helping to minimize public debt charges. It is also in the interest of other public and private sector borrowers who could be affected if government borrowing operations were distorted, and will assist government policies to support the continuing smooth functioning of both the financial and the exchange markets. As some members may know, Section 39 of the Financial Administration Act permits the Government to raise funds with terms to maturity not to exceed six months if, in the opinion of the Governor in Council, there will be insufficient funds to meet disbursements.
In the event that Section 39 is used, I would not wish that its use result in authority to borrow more than I am requesting in the bill currently before this House. Therefore, I would be prepared to amend the bill at committee stage to deduct from the $5 billion sought for this year any amounts borrowed under Section 39. In any case, Section 39 is an emergency-measure and is not designed for long-term use. The Government would be extremely limited in its debt operations since it would be able to raise new funds only through the issue of three- and six-month Treasury bills.
The sale of one-year Treasury bills and bonds has been and will continue to be a major source of funds for the Government. Use of these sources is not possible under Section 39.
While I have put considerable emphasis on the need to carry out the government's borrowing operations in a business-like and cost-effective manner, I would not wish to leave members with the impression that I lack confidence in the strength and flexibility of Canada's financial markets. The people working in the Canadian financial markets are among the most skilled and resourceful in the world. Our financial markets have in the past shown a great ability to adapt to meet changing demands placed upon them. This view of the financial markets has been confirmed in my consultations with business and financial people when I have asked for their advice on the risks of crowding out in the debt markets because of the high government borrowings. Canada continues to have an extremely high savings rate-13 per cent of disposable income-which supports the view that our capital markets are equal to the task. One might add that the best evidence to date for this view is that interest rates have fallen dramatically even during a period of heavy government borrowing. Let me emphasize again, however, that any disruption in the Government's debt program caused by delay in passing this legislation will risk unnecessary public debt charges and inconvenience for other public and private sector borrowers.
As I have made clear, government has a responsibility to provide support to economic activity through the deficit in times such as these. But government has an equal responsibility not to impede the private sector from playing its role as the
February 17, 1983

main engine of economic growth in the recovery period that lies ahead.
So, while Honourable Members may share my concern about the government's debt program, an even greater concern is the health and vitality of the private sector. It is of course impossible to link the funds borrowed by government to specific expenditures. However, I have already outlined the major causes of the increased financial requirements, and they are part and parcel of the impact of the recession which the deficit has served to cushion. Likewise, in the next few months, the Government faces heavy spending commitments arising out of measures designed to ease that impact. In addition, in the next few months the Government will have to pay out more than $6 billion in tax refunds-a source of considerable immediate stimulus to the economy in its own right. I would remind Honourable Members that timely payment of refunds depends on approval of the income tax legislation which I mentioned earlier as one of the vital steps to economic stability. There is thus added urgency in getting on with the task at hand over and above the need for orderly and efficient management of the debt program.
Before closing, I want to emphasize that financial requirements have risen because of unexpectedly harsh cyclical forces. The Government of Canada remains committed to its longer term goal of systematic restraint of its expenditures as a proportion of the GNP, and to systematic reduction of the deficit as well. It is important to recognize that substantial reductions in the deficit were achieved in fiscal years 1979-80, 1980-81 and 1981-82, as illustrated by the fact that the Government's financial requirements dropped from a level equivalent to 4.8 per cent of GNP in 1978-79 to only 2.5 per cent of GNP in 1981-82. The weak economic situation at the present time has seriously eroded Government revenues and inflated Government expenditures; a strong recovery would obviously have the opposite effect.
Canada has suffered an extremely severe recession. Tax bases have fallen and unemployment has risen. The fiscal position is very sensitive to economic conditions and has been dramatically affected by these developments. We must keep these matters in proper perspective when interpreting the present deficit level.
I might add that in my consultations during recent months, there has been strong support from a wide range of groups for continued restraint by Government, particularly as exemplified by the six and five program. Yet while there has been widely shared concern about the deficit, no one has asked me to cut away the safety nets for those truly in need. Nor was I asked to increase greatly the burden of taxation at this time. There is wide agreement that the best way to reduce the deficit is to support the economy through this difficult period and return as quickly as possible to economic growth.
Borrowing Authority
Our plans have been dealt a severe blow-no question about it. So have those of virtually all Canadians. The temporary increase in the deficit to help those who need help the most is playing a vital role in maintaining the strength needed to provide a base for economic recovery. It is time for all of us to play our part in building up that strength and that recovery in the months and years ahead.
I therefore invite Hon. Members to address this Bill at long last on second reading. We will have an opportunity to debate it in the House and to consider it at committee stage. There will be opportunity for full debate on the Income Tax Act, which has been before the House for some time and has already been the subject not only of extensive consideration by a parliamentary committee for many weeks since last fall but has also been examined by the House for several days, on second reading.
I have indicated the importance of addressing this issue in a responsible and expeditious way in order to ensure that we will have a debt management program that will be efficient, will involve the least possible cost to the taxpayer and cause the least possible disruption of financial markets.
The money required for the rest of this year has been fully explained. I have indicated why the money is required, what the financial situation of the Government is for 1982-83, and that the additional amount of $14 billion for 1983-84 is required as an interim payment. After my budget, I intend to introduce another borrowing authority Bill which will cover the full 1983-84 period. At that time Parliament will have a full opportunity to examine the total requirement of the Government in 1983-84 in light of the budget that I will present and the Estimates that will be presented to the House on February 22. Parliament will, therefore, have before it all the facts that it needs to make a decision in the full knowledge of the implications of the various decisions that are required.
As far as the Bill is concerned, it is quite clear. I do not think I need add much to what I have already said.

I therefore invite the House to give serious consideration to and expedite the passage of a Bill that is of vital importance to ensure that our country's economic recovery, which has now started, will continue, to prevent problems on the financial market and to provide for sound and effective management of the public debt. The funds borrowed by the Government will benefit Canadians. As I said before, these funds are mainly borrowed on the domestic market and are used to finance Government programs aimed mainly at easing the impact of the recession on many Canadians, especially on those drawing unemployment insurance benefits, those on welfare and those benefiting from the Government's direct job creation programs. These sums are also necessary because as a result of the recession, both individuals and corporations are paying less in taxes than they were paying when wages and corporate profits were higher.

February 17, 1983
Borrowing Authority
I hope now that economic recovery has started it will continue throughout 1983. According to our projections, inflation will continue to drop, and economic growth is expected to accelerate in the course of the year as incomes of private citizens and corporations increase. When this happens, government revenues, and the Canadian Government's revenues in particular, will increase as well, making it easier for the Government to reduce the deficit and the substantial financial requirements it cannot avoid at the present time if it is to take at all seriously its responsibility as a Government, during a recession as serious as the one we have experienced.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with a great deal of sadness and distress that I address the House today. That sadness and distress is more explicit because the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) is afraid or unwilling, or both, to give to the House the financial projection that it is entitled to receive. We have received no tables, no statements, no projections with respect to unemployment, with respect to the deficit in the Unemployment Insurance Fund or with respect to what is happening with the Established Programs Financing Act which he says is paying out more money. That Act is somehow tied to a floating GNP rate.
We have no idea why the Minister wants a $2 billion nonlapsing borrowing authority for next year. He pulls out of the air a need for $5 billion, which he says he will have to borrow within six weeks because the year end is March 31. Yet he refuses to explain himself. He refuses to answer questions. But what does he say to this House and to the people of Canada? He says: "Trust us."
Yesterday we found out how we should trust the Liberals, and this Minister who signs agreements that make sure a friend of his gets a fee of $600 a day. The Minister has told us about the people who are unemployed. He has told us about the employment programs of this Government. What about the $800 a day for a former Minister? What about $450 a day for a former candidate? These are the very important employment programs?
The Minister said he did not have time to settle in because of the quicksand, but he has settled this country in quicksand, and he knows it.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 (NO. 3) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: Don't forget the National Energy Program.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 (NO. 3) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH

The Minister said Chairman Mao was concerned about forecasting. I thought that remark in his speech, comparing his activities to the activities of Chairman Mao was rather interesting. The forecast cannot be given to us because it is Chairman Mao's operation perhaps that is running this Government.
We do not have any figures, sir. We are asked, because of the condition of the financial markets, to rubberstamp a Bill which, in total, gives the Government of Canada the authority to borrow an amount of $19 billion against the credit of Canada. We have a Minister who refuses to stand up in this House and answer questions. That is unforgivable.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 (NO. 3) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: That is not what he said.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 (NO. 3) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
It is totally wrong and it is not the kind of thing that we should expect from any Government.
Let me remind the Minister of what his predecessor said to the Standing Committee of Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs in May, 1982. I shall now read his statement into the record. The then Minister of Finance said this:
I would not expect the House to act upon an additional request for borrowing authority without providing it with detailed information on the economic situation and the implications of that situation on the government's fiscal situation. I do not think it would be appropriate to ask the House for additional borrowing authority until I have laid out in some detail an update of both the economic situation and the fiscal situation, and I certainly will be doing that before I would come back to the House for additional borrowing authority.
That has been the pattern of all responsible Governments, all responsible Ministers, until now, until yesterday, until today. We have a Minister who says: "Trust us; we want $19 billion, trust us". But every projection and everything he has said to date leaves us with no ground whatsoever on which to trust him.
February 17, 1983

Canadians are pretty concerned because the Minister says the only thing that is holding up the country is Bill C-139, and somewhere along the line the passage of that income tax Bill, which significantly increases taxes, will somehow make it possible for this whole problem of borrowing to go away. That does not make sense.
If you have a situation where both the economy and business in the country are turned off, how would you expect to turn them on again by increasing small business taxes by 12.5 per cent, by reducing capital cost allowances in the first year by 50 per cent and by limiting interest deductions for new capital expenditure? Indeed, how would you expect any businessman to want to go ahead and expand when facing him is Bill C-139, a most destructive Bill, a most disincentive-minded Bill, one that is anti-entrepreneurial, anti-growth and anti-business? Yet this Minister talks about the private economy being the engine of growth, and he asks us to trust him.
The Minister has taken us down a garden path which is a garden path over quicksand, Mr. Speaker. He has talked about quicksand. Let us talk about the quicksand in which he has put this country.
First, the amount of this borrowing Bill will destroy confidence in this country. There is no question that this Government is now asking us to approve borrowings, presumably unlimited borrowings, because $19 billion, he says, will only last him until this summer. The Minister is asking us to approve borrowings that amount to nearly $1 billion a week from now until the end of June. He says that will give us confidence to build the country, to make it grow.
He also says he is not going to crowd out the business field. Let us examine that. On a current basis, the personal savings this year are somewhere around $31 billion per annum. That is not $19 billion between now and the end of June; that is $31 billion for the whole year. Between now and the end of June personal savings are nowhere close to the amount required by this Government.
The Government has been helped recently because there have been some corporate savings as a result of a depression in the corporate field. Business has been turned off; inventories have been depressed. Therefore, some savings have been generated from the lessening of business activities in the country. But that is not likely to continue. Indeed, if it does, if the business community continues its net savings, heaven help our opportunities for employment in the country.
This Bill and the Government's borrowing requirements, on top of Government borrowing requirements from all Provinces-and I remind the House that even the Province of Alberta, previously a Province which generated huge surpluses, is now out in the market looking for money-will, in fact, crowd out business and people who want to borrow to expand, to build homes, to build plants and to provide jobs. This Bill is the expropriation of virtually all the savings in the country to finance Government. It would be all right if the Government were using money in a productive fashion, but we all know that this Government is really a great consumer, a great spender
Borrowing Authority
for consumption, rather than the spender for the creation of capital, new work, new buildings and new projects. This country's savings are being taken by the Government and spent on consumption. If we allow this to happen, it will prevent any recovery from this depression. I say depression, not recession, because that is our situation today. The Government has failed to devise any program or give any direction to ameliorate the depression in any way or give us any hope or confidence for the future.
Some say that Government spending and borrowing is stimulative. I would remind the House that when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was first elected in 1968, the Government deficit was $497 million. There were 358,000 people unemployed. The Minister has told us today that his deficit for this year will be very close to $27.5 billion, or $27,500 million. Unemployment today is at 1.6 million or 1.7 million. How many people are discouraged or really are not working? How many are involved in worksharing or are on training programs? Those people are not working either. Therefore, what is the real unemployment figure? Perhaps it is 2 million or 2.5 million. The Government said unemployment is at 1.6 million, but what is the real figure?
Has the Government's borrowing been in any way stimulative? The answer is no. In fact, it has been one of the main factors that has led to the destruction of employment and the destruction of the hopes and dreams of Canadians.
We must remember that interest must be paid on money that is borrowed. If $5 billion is borrowed at 12 per cent interest, it means that $10 billion is needed to pay back in five years. This borrowing Bill which asks for $19 billion means that $38 billion will be paid in five years, if it is paid back by then. If it is not, it doubles in the next five years and doubles again in the five years after that. That is where the Government is headed when it introduces one borrowing Bill after another.
We now see the introduction of borrowing Bills that do not give us any projections. We do not see any projections because, if the Government projected its future borrowing requirements and the interest it would have to pay on that money without any possibility of paying it back, Canadians would rise up and throw the Government out. I say that Canadians will rise up and throw the Government out. We must throw the Government out because it has destroyed our system. It has destroyed our business sector and has destroyed the hopes and dreams of many Canadians. It is now in the process of destroying our financial system completely. Our financial system cannot realistically support the debt which the Government is asking us to approve.
We are often asked what we would do if we were in Government.

speechtext:
A year ago we told the Government that it was about time that a committee of the House was formed to seriously set the priorities for Government spending, to eliminate all but the most absolutely essential expenditures. That view was echoed by the Auditor General in his Report to the House last fall. It was further echoed in a proposal made by the Canadian Chamber of Commerce in their pre-budget submissions to the Minister.
The fact of the matter is that the situation has become most serious. The Minister says that his revenues are down and that 72 per cent of his problems are a result of decreasing revenue. The answer to those problems is that we must set our priorities straight and at some point come to grips with whether our priorities are for old age pensions or VIA Rail. We may have to come to grips with whether it is parks or payments made to people under the Canada Assistance Plan. We are getting to the point where we can no longer finance the budget with these kinds of requirements.
There is no question that it is acceptable to borrow money over a short period if one is able to pay it back. However, money cannot be borrowed year after year when there is no possibility of paying it back. There is no hope to pay back the money being asked for in this borrowing Bill.
We are told that the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray) will produce his Estimates on February 22. I suggest it is about time that he did so. 1 hope those Estimates will effectively reduce some of the Government's costs. I hope those Estimates will eliminate some of those troughs from which money is drawn by program after program to pay for more administrators, more forms and more patronage jobs-the CHIP, the NIP, the DIP and a host of others. There is a volume of programs that requires administrators and people to review those programs that, when analyzed, may be desirable but not totally necessary. The House of Commons must come to grips with our spending to keep it more in line with our ability and the ability of the country to meet those expenditures. Until we accomplish that, people will not be employed again, Canadians will not be able to own their own homes and the confidence in our country will not be restored. Our nation will not be built. We should be talking here about building our nation.
A nation cannot be built by trying to borrow itself rich. No one has ever borrowed themselves rich. You do not print yourself rich either.

My friend from Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans) says that it depends on what you do with the borrowing. Let us examine what is done with the borrowing. It is mostly spent on the interest from previous borrowings. The Government has to borrow more money all the time just to pay the interest. The last projection we saw included $17 billion in interest. We do not know what the current projection is because we do not get one. We do not get a projection because the Minister is afraid to give it to us.
As we proceed with this borrowing Bill, we see a further erosion of the tax base in the country. The Minister said in his press release that his tax receipts are down. He says that he will therefore have to borrow the money to make up for that reduction. In any business, if one's income is down one does not go to the banker and say: "Because my income is down I have to borrow more money". Bankers will throw you out. That is what we have to do with the Government. We have to throw it out. The Government cannot tell us that its revenue is down and therefore, since it cannot possibly cut its spending, it must borrow the money for its expenditures. That is just incredible. There must be some relationship between borrowing and the ability to pay it back. Payback of this borrowing is impossible.
What we really have here is a Government which no longer has the support of the people of Canada. Forty-nine per cent of the people of Canada replying to a Gallup poll indicated that they do not want this Government. They want another Government, a Government composed of people from this side of the House. The Government and the Minister of Finance know that. However, rather than let the people of Canada have their way in a general election, which the people of Canada now want and need because of the Government's profligate waste, it has entered a scorched earth policy. With its tax measures, its bureaucracy, its regulation and its control, it is destroying businesses. With its attitudes-the way in which it looks after its friends and runs a fat trough, the way it operates without giving any projections or basis for sound economic belief, management and leadership, which it should be supplying-it destroys public confidence. Now with this Bill and its management of the economy of the country, it is destroying the very financial system itself. Its attitude seems to be that, if it cannot govern, no one else will govern because there will be no country left to govern. That is the way it goes about it. That attitude is what we must stop, and we must stop it in this House of Commons now.

A capital market account written by Hugh Anderson for yesterday's Financial Times, of Canada, indicated the following:
It's one thing to talk glibly about financing $30 billion deficits, but it is another thing to actually see it done. We're looking at a federal issue every three

or four weeks, which means the provinces will have to rush in somewhere between, whenever the market seems firm enough.
What this means is that anybody who wants to buy bonds this year will have plenty to choose from. There will be no need to chase a rising market. As they say about the bus you just missed, there'll be another one along in a minute.
It is a rush-hour all right. It is a rush-hour for the Minister to go out to the markets of this country to borrow the kind of money he is talking about in the Bill. It is that very rush-hour attitude toward borrowing that we on this side cannot tolerate.
Imagine the nerve in saying to the House of Commons, "Here is a Bill for $19 billion. I do not have any projections, fellas. Maybe I will make a budget, maybe I will give you some projections then, but in the meantime, trust me and ram it through in a hurry, because if you do not, you will upset the financial requirements of the country and will make me use Section 39 of the Financial Administration Act, and perhaps somewhere along the line we will have to pay more for our money than we would otherwise."
That is not believable. On the very face of it, it is incredible. The Government, by presenting the Bill in the fashion it has, has lost the moral right to govern.

Mr. Speaker, it is with very little pleasure that I rise to speak to Bill C-143 today. We have just witnessed a spectacle in the House of Commons today with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) standing and asking the people of Canada, through the Members of this House, to approve the borrowing of another $19 billion.
I am afraid that the Government, most recently through the Minister of Finance, has presented us with a horror story and has turned the House of Commons into a house of horrors. He has turned Parliament into a horror house and, quite frankly-

-the people of Canada will find out from newscasts later today that the Minister of Finance is asking for additional borrowing authority which will push the deficit projection up to $27.2 billion, up 16 per cent from October. That is a 16 per cent error in four months. If there is anything that clearly demonstrates to the people of Canada that the Government is completely out of control when it comes to fiscal management, a 16 per cent error in four months must certainly do so.
To add insult to injury, the Minister tells us in his statement that next year the Government will abandon its six and five program. It has spent hundreds of thousands of dollars in fancy brochures sent to every person who would consider picking one up, and many people who would not even consider it, saying that it wants everyone in the country to follow the six and five restraint program. It has passed Bills in the House providing that Family Allowances will be restricted to 6 per cent this year and 5 per cent next year so that the mothers and children of Canada will have their expected incomes restricted to 6 per cent. Senior citizens receiving Old Age Security will not receive an increase reflecting the rate of inflation, keeping

their measly pensions at the existing level. The Government will restrict those increases to 6 per cent and 5 per cent. The same is true concerning retired Armed Forces and RCMP personnel as well as retired civil servants.
The Minister of Finance came into the House of Commons today and said: "Folks, we have great news for Canadians. We will jack the deficit up now by an additional 16 per cent from what we thought back in October, up to $27.2 billion, and next year our expected expenditures will be in excess of 9.6 per cent. Abandon six and five. Our revenues will be up by at least 9.6 per cent." Mark my words, Mr. Speaker. Based on the ability to project which has been demonstrated by Hon. Members opposite with their senior civil servants advising them, if they say that it is expected that expenditures will be up by 9.6 per cent next year, we know that that is an error, virtually by definition.
Yes, the Government has created a horror House of Commons. I have listened to the Minister of Finance representing the Government and saying: "I want Hon. Members opposite to listen carefully to me because they might learn a few things". Can one imagine a more unlikely instructor, teacher, professor or guru than the Minister of Finance, who has been telling Hon. Members opposite to listen carefully, to learn about fiscal management? My goodness! That is like asking Jesse James to advise on banking or Clifford Olson to advise on parenting skills. This man opposite, masquerading as Minister of Finance, has turned this place into a theatre of the absurd.
The people of Canada are going to be out there today listening to what is coming out of this House on the Government side, shaking their heads in disbelief and saying that they cannot believe that this Government is adding $5 billion more without saying a single word about how it is going to spend those funds. Then it says it has another great idea; it is going to ask for an extra $14 billion. $14 billion, $15 billion, $25 billion, who cares?
I remember when not six months ago the then Minister of Finance stood in his place and projected a deficit of up to $23 billion plus. At that time I said I would not be a bit surprised if, when the final results come in on this deficit raise, it will be closer to $30 billion. Members opposite howled and laughed and scoffed and said: "What a dreamer; what an unbelievable projection that is!" Yet we have the Minister of Finance rising today and saying that the best guesstimate of the Government at this time is $27.2 billion. Mr. Speaker, we know that the deficit is going to be higher than that. We know absolutely that it is going to be higher than that.
Let me talk positively for a moment about the Minister's speech. He spoke for 45 minutes and when I listened to those 45 minutes of delivery I identified two statements that I thought were of a positive nature.

He had the day right, my colleague for Saskatoon East Mr. Ogle says. He did not have his figures correct because, as he admitted, he has been so far out in any projections and virtually all of the projection houses have been so far out that we can ignore them, and he said he was going to predict that next year things were going to get better anyway. I think that his credibility and the Government's credibility has gone the way of the dodo bird. It is no longer here.
However, to give credit where credit is due, the Minister of Finance said that the deficit would be used for contributions to Unemployment Insurance extended benefits. We in this Party say that is a positive move. It is a desperate move but it is positive. It is going to ease the pain for literally hundreds of thousands of Canadians-one could almost say millions of Canadians. Almost 2 million Canadians will listen to this news with some glee. Also he said that this deficit that he is asking us to support in principle today includes a $240 million adjustment to cover anticipated additional requirements under the Canadian Home Ownership Stimulation Program. We say that that is positive as well. Apart from those two statements in 45 minutes of delivery, that is it. I cannot think of another positive thing to say about what the Minister of Finance has said in this House this morning.
Not only is this situation in which Canadians find themselves today a fiscal disaster but it is a human disaster, a human calamity. We hear all kinds of things about $14 billion here, $5 billion there, the need to strengthen the dollar and so on. In other words, a total delivery using numbers in terms that 90 per cent of Canadians do not understand. But I notice that he did not once refer to the people of Canada. He did not once refer to the hardships that millions of people in this country are experiencing today. He did not refer to the pain of people sitting at home who have been unemployed for months and months and know that they are about to go on welfare unless something happens, so they listen to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) today to see what is going to happen. And what does he tell us? He does not tell us a single thing about what is going to happen. He just says: "Give us more money, that is all that I ask for".
That is like my young son, who is 12 years old, saying to his father: "Dad, I want to borrow $200". I would say: "That is interesting, son, but what are you going to use that $200 for? Are you trying a little business venture? Are you going to do some investing? Do you want to purchase something?" He replies: "Dad, I am not telling; just give me $200. I am not going to tell you what I am going to use it for. Trust me." I trust my son but I would have a little reluctance in falling over myself to give my son $200 to spend as he deems appropriate, without some discussion.
Can you imagine a small businessman, a farmer or fisherman going to his bank or credit union and saying: "I want to borrow $200,000. I need this money. Please, let us sign the papers." Of course, the banker or the financier would ask: "What is this money going to be used for? How are you going to invest it? What is your cash flow? What is your marketing strategy? What is your track record? How many people are
employed? How are you going to approach the sales?" If that businessman said: "I am not going to tell you anything. I have no idea how I am going to spend $200,000 but I sure would like it", the banker would say to that small businessman, farmer or fisherman what we are saying to the Minister of Finance-"Forget it, because we are not going to give you authority to spend taxpayers' money"-

-"to go out and borrow $14 billion plus $5 billion without telling us a single thing about how it is going to be spent".
Do Government Members think we are dodos over here, that we are going to stand here and give them authority to do that? I am looking forward to their speeches a little later, to listen to how on earth they are going to explain to the people of Canada why the Government is going to ask for $19 billion without telling us how it is going to spend it.
Perhaps it will say that it will rely on its track record. If a small businessman used that approach when seeking money and said: "Just look at my track record; I have been a dismal failure for the last decade", again we will respond as that banker would respond. We will say that that is not good enough, that we are not prepared to give that kind of support today and we are not prepared to give that kind of support tomorrow.
I said, Mr. Speaker, that this was not only the beginning of a fiscal calamity or disaster, it is a human disaster. There is an old Hindu proverb that says: "Where there is no dream, the people perish". That Canadian dream has now become a Canadian nightmare and the people are perishing. Canadians are despairing from one end of this country to the other. It can be seen in their eyes. When one visits a hard-pressed part of the Third World, as my colleague for Saskatoon East has many times, and walks the streets talking to groups of people, there is a sense often of despair in the people's eyes. They have struggled for 40 years of their lives trying to raise their families, only to find that the corruption in those countries often makes it impossible for them to succeed. They eventually get that hollow look in their eyes, that depressed look, that sad look, that look of "I have given up".
One can look at pictures of people during the 1930s in our country, during the depth of the Depression, and see that same hollow look in their eyes. One sees in pictures of refugee camps today that same hopeless look in their eyes, that emptiness. That is what we are seeing in Canada today.
I think the most disappointing experience I have had in the last few weeks was when I was visiting a number of secondary schools in my constituency to talk to the graduating classes, only to find that those young people are saying: "What is the use? Why should I continue to study hard and go on to a postsecondary education when almost everyone I know is either out of work or will be shortly? Why should I study hard in my schooling? What is the hope of struggling and going on? What is the purpose? My father has worked 20 years in a plant and
February 17, 1983

is now laid off; he is 54 years of age and likely will not get a job again. My brother who has completed university is driving cabs because he cannot find a job in the computer industry."
That is the kind of weight, Mr. Speaker, that is coming down on the shoulders of Canadians; but, most important, it is coming down on the shoulders of Canada's youth. In Canada's youth is Canada's future, and that depression, that weight and despair are pulling down that group at the age when they should be full of zest, life and vitality. Exactly the opposite is happening. I emphasize that part of the reason is the actions of this Government and the kind of statement it is making to the people of Canada through Bill C-143.
The people of Canada have been losing faith in their elected representatives and in their Governments. I suspect that if the popularity level of many politicians today was to be evaluated, they would be at the bottom of the heap along with child molesters, tax collectors and the like. Why is that? What is happening? When we look at the record of this Government, it becomes very clear.
We have two million people out of work. We have thousands and thousands more going on welfare because their Unemployment Insurance benefits are terminating. Employees are under incredible stress because of cutbacks and the resultant additional workload. People are experiencing burn-out and overwork more than ever before. They are struggling to make ends meet. Single parents are attempting to raise children on an income of $9,000 a year. By and large, the senior citizens of this country live below the poverty level in spite of what the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) says about the floating poverty line.
With this kind of situation, with people tense and concerned about the future for themselves and their children, the Prime Minister says: "Shucks, all Canadians are skiing or down in the Caribbean on beaches". What does that tell us about the Prime Minister? He has not only lost touch with the people of Canada but with reality. If he thinks that Canadians are doing one of two things, either skiing or on beaches in the Caribbean, any psychiatrist will tell you that is a clear indication that this man, who is presumably leading our land, has lost touch with the real world. There are not many people from the constituency of Kamloops-Shuswap who have money to spend on the ski slopes or on holidays on Caribbean beaches. Virtually no one there is in either of those two categories.
This is the same man who thinks it is a good idea to limit the income of pensioners, to limit the income of families through Family Allowance restrictions, and to give the chairman of the task force looking into the state of the economy $800 a day, plus expenses. When travelling across the country, he will get much more than that. The Prime Minister thinks that is appropriate. That is more than senior citizens get to live on for an entire month. The Prime Minister thinks it is appropriate in these times of restraint and difficulty to give that individual $800 a day plus.

It is very clear that our Prime Minister never goes door-knocking in his constituency or those of others. He never sits in coffee shops and talks to normal folk. He does not sit in pubs and talk to those who work in the mines, plants and offices of this country. He does not talk to normal people.
The Prime Minister of Canada does not speak to normal Canadians. He speaks to the high-powered group of advisers around him, the senior lobbyists, senior mandarins, people who are not struggling and are not threatened by job loss, the Ian Sinclairs of the world. That man is quite prepared to take a 6 per cent restriction of his increase, which will be in excess of $50,000 for the next year.
It is a dark day for Canada when we have to look to an individual to provide leadership during these very difficult times who has lost touch with reality. One begins to wonder whether that same loss of touch has not rubbed off on other members of his Cabinet when we find the Minister of Finance standing in his place and asking us to push through post-haste $19 billion so that they can get on with the job. Some job he wants to get on with!
The people of Canada are having a difficult time supporting with enthusiasm this present Government. Government Members have criss-crossed Canada asking people to restrain, introducing monetary policies that force people to restrain. Now they have changed their minds and are criss-crossing the country asking people to spend, invest and expand. You cannot go out one day and ask people to cut back and restrain, and then get on the next plane and ask them to spend, borrow and expand.
In his darkest moments before going to sleep at night, I am sure the Minister of Finance wonders why the people of Canada are not expanding their plants, factories and firms. The reason is that they have lost faith in the political leadership of this country. There is only one way to change that. In order to bolster and build confidence in the future of this country, we have a big task at hand, namely to change the leadership of this country. 1 want to say that it is time for a new vision.

This should be done after a great deal of consultation with all levels of Government-federal, provincial, regional, local-and proper consultations between management and labour. That would provide the people of this country with a vision of what Canada should and could be.
Canadians know in their hearts that they live in the richest country on earth, a country with more natural resources per capita than any country on the face of this globe. Here we are struggling and stumbling over ourselves as the Government lurches from crisis to crisis. The Official Opposition are

Borrowing Authority
running at each other with swords trying to impale and disembowel each other. We wonder why people have lost confidence. I suggest that we consider an alternative. I wonder if it would be proper for me to move a motion at this point regarding the Bill before us. I would move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Kootenay East-Revelstoke (Mr. Parker):
That this Bill be not read the second time until after February 22, when we have had time to examine the tabling of the Main Estimates for the fiscal year 1983-84.
I have indicated very clearly that it is time in this country for a new vision. Canadians in their hearts and souls know what this country can be. It is time to put fear and uncertainty behind us and take steps to see what Canada can be and ought to be. It is time we faced the future head on with a bold innovative and creative program for the future of our country.
One of the guideposts, Mr. Speaker, which we must include in such a vision is a commitment in this country to full employment. With the small population which Canada has and its abundant resources in both natural, human and financial terms, there is no reason why we cannot set as a realistic goal full employment for Canada.
We are at a very critical point in our economic history right now, Mr. Speaker, where we are either going to advance or retreat, and, unfortunately, we have to look to the Members opposite to give us either the direction to advance or to bring in policies which will guarantee a collapse of the economy in this country.
I heard the Minister of Finance earlier talk about the future and I remembered distinctly reading in Hansard the comments which the various Ministers were making in 1930. It seemed like deja vu, Mr. Speaker. In 1930 Government Members were standing up and saying: "Things are about to turn around. We are optimistic. Indicators point to an economic upturn. We have confidence in the future. We are not going to do anything, but we have confidence."
Unfortunately, that is exactly the point at which Canadians find themselves today. We must now launch an energetic program of recovery which will have full employment as part of its mandate. It will involve the co-operation of all regions of Canada, as well as the various sectors of the economy, both in economic terms as well as political. We must make a commitment to retain the existing social programs which are in place and to build and improve on them. We must no longer allow ourselves to be an appendage to the economy of some other country.
We realize that to accomplish these goals there will be costs which Canadians are going to be asked to share. There will be some very difficult times in accomplishing these goals. But the sacrifices, Mr. Speaker, must be made on the basis of equality. Fighting a war on inflation or building a recovery program must not be done on the backs of Canada's unemployed. It must not be done on the backs of Canada's women or Canada's minority groups, as the present Government is doing at this time. It must be done on an equal basis, and that means we
must continue to oppose Bill C-139, a Bill to amend the Income Tax Act, because it perpetrates an injustice in this country. That Bill is telling Canadians that taxes will be increased for low and middle-income groups but will be decreased for the wealthy, and that is something, Mr. Speaker, that the Hon. Members of this House must oppose until their dying breath. That kind of injustice will make economic recovery impossible in this country.
Another factor which will make economic recovery in this country impossible is that there are two million people out of work. This figure is growing by the week and, by the Minister of Finance's own admission, will continue to grow during 1983. It is impossible to have economic recovery in this country with the albatross of two million unemployed around the neck of our economy, and it will be impossible until the Government addresses that problem head on.
The Government's priorities in the upcoming budget must be three-fold-jobs, jobs and more jobs. It will be a clear signal to Canadians that this Government means business and that it is going to get the economy moving once again when it deals, along with its recovery package, with the serious unemployment situation.
We in the New Democratic Party have a concern about this deficit. We see it as an unproductive deficit because it is unplanned. I remember the previous Leader of the Progressive Conservative Party supporting something he called, I believe, a "stimulative" deficit. We would like to see the Minister of Finance stand up and clearly demonstrate how this increased deficit will eventually result in a reduced deficit. I would like to hear the Minister of Finance say: "If we are going to go into a deficit situation, this is our recovery plan. This is the way we are investing these borrowed funds to result in an eventual return to the people of Canada." But he does not say that, Mr. Speaker, and we know that this money is not being invested in economic recovery infrastructure. This deficit is just continuing more frivolous Government spending, by and large.
If it is not, then I would beg the Hon. Members opposite to stand in their places and explain how this additional $19 billion of borrowing is going to result in eventual economic return to Canadians. A deficit per se is not necessarily a disaster. Every businessman knows it is sound business practice to borrow money and invest it in order to get a return. That is what the New Democratic Party has been saying for some time, that if we are going to borrow money, let us ensure it is wisely invested, at least.
In terms of planning for a deficit, I believe it is critical that we, as Parliamentarians, realize that our economy in this country is at a crucial turning point, that where our economy went down in a recession or depression, most of it is going to be coming back in a different location. The economy of the 1980s and 1990s will be significantly different from the economy of the 1960s and 1970s.
I ask Hon. Members opposite whether they realize the incredible economic transition and revolution which is going on in this country at this point, because I see no evidence that they do. During this excellent opportunity for the Minister of
February 17, 1983

Finance to give the people of Canada a demonstration that the Government understands the significance of this economic turmoil and is prepared to deal with it, for him not to utter a single phrase, which would indicate the Government understands what is happening to the Canadian economy, I think is tragic. It is unforgivable. If the people of Canada had a thread of hope and the Government had a thread of credibility left, it has been ripped apart today.
It is interesting, Mr. Speaker-now that the Minister of State for Economic Development (Mr. Johnston) has arrived-to find that we have just completed a so-called agreement with the Japanese auto industry. I want to say to the Minister that a small country like Trinidad, which welcomes the import of automobiles because it does not make any of its own, said to the Japanese companies: "You can sell all the Japanese vehicles, including trucks, in our country that you like, but you have to assemble not 20 per cent, not 50 per cent but 100 per cent of those vehicles in our country. We want to create employment for our people in Trinidad."
The Japanese companies went along with this, Mr. Speaker. That is a country with a population of 1.2 million people. Here in Canada we have 24 million people, the seventh major trading country of the world for the Japanese auto industry, and we do not have them assemble a single automobile in Canada. What kind of negotiating, what kind of planning, is that?
In summary, let me say that the Minister of Finance missed a golden opportunity today to present the Government's game plan strategy to the people of Canada, to tell the people of Canada how the Government would be using this borrowed money for their benefit. He said nothing. My closing comment, Mr. Speaker, is that we have been asked to buy a pig in a poke and we are not buying it.

Borrowing Authority

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 (NO. 3) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have before us today a request by the Government to borrow an unprecedented amount of money to pay unspecified bills for programs which are not yet clearly identified. The $19 billion which the Government is seeking to borrow represents a Government which is bankrupt in terms of revenue, bankrupt in terms of ideas and policies, and bankrupt in terms of moral authority to impose this kind of burden on the Canadian taxpayer.
This blank cheque which we have before us, and which we are asked to authorize, represents nothing more than an unwanted legacy for the next Government of Canada, which will be a Conservative Government. It is an attempt by the Government to put off to the future the difficult task of paying for the debts run up by a Government which has proved itself incapable of managing the country's economic affairs.
Taxpayers should clearly understand that borrowings of this size represent a deferred tax increase on them, a tax increase that taxpayers will inevitably have to assume. It represents a constraint on this Government's ability to govern and on future Governments' ability to set national priorities for years to come. It represents the legacy of a Government which has clearly washed its hands of any attempt to manage the economy in a credible manner, and instead is dumping the entire responsibility for the economic problems facing this country on to the backs of the overburdened taxpayer in the future.
Finance Minister Lalonde insists that this huge borrowing authority is required to underwrite the costs borne by the recession. His assumption is clearly that borrowings on such a huge scale, which amount to claims on Canada's economic future, will help resolve the economic problems facing us. If that were in fact the case, we would be much more receptive to his demands. But Mr. Lalonde-

speechtext:
-does not make this case based on any evidence. I recently completed a trip through the interior of my home Province, British Columbia. It was a sombre experience in the sombre season of mid-winter. In the towns I visited the lumber mills are silent, the mines are shut down, the motels and restaurants are nearly empty. "For sale" signs and foreclosure notices sprout forlornly along the streets which are subdued and quiet. There is an uneasy absence of activity. Now, we would like to think that these billions sought by the Government will help restore some life to these centres. However, there is little indication they will.
Like other MPs, I continually deal with the problems of the unemployed who stop us in supermarkets, on the streets, in the coffee shops, asking for advice. They want to know what to do when their Unemployment Insurance benefits run out. They want to know how to survive until their welfare cheques are processed. Most of all, they want to know when there will be an end to all this economic stress. But again, there is no indication when faced with this Bill that it contains any answers except to borrow, borrow and borrow again.

February 17, 1983
Borrowing A uthority
All across the country the silent plants, the business failures, the fire sales, equipment auctions and the half-excavated apartment sites are mute testimony to the failure of this Government to address the real problems faced by the economy. These real problems stem from deep structural changes. These changes include the probability that some of the mines of this country will never reopen. Half the labour force in the mining industry is out of work. There is a grim realization in the construction and forest industries that many of the people who are now out of work will never return to their jobs. There is a growing fear that many of our young people may spend the best part of their youth looking for job opportunities which are simply not there. None of these problems is addressed in this Bill seeking the authority to borrow $19 billion.
Any creditor who went to any financial institution in this country seeking this kind of credit or financial borrowing without giving more details on how the money will be spent, and more importantly how the money will be repaid, would be refused by any responsible financial institution. Yet this Government is asking for its second borrowing authority Bill in three and a half months. It is asking for $5 billion in supplementary borrowing authority for the current fiscal year which ends in six weeks' time, and for $14 billion in interim borrowing authority for the next fiscal year, 1983-84, which the Minister suggests might last him until mid-summer. It is asking for this scale of borrowing at a time when many small businessmen in this country have had their lines of credit slashed and which face the mercenary practices of the Department of National Revenue, which is squeezing every dime out of every pocket, out of every bank account, out of every receivable it can lay its hands on.
The irresponsibility shown by this Government and its arrogance in seeking this kind of borrowing authority without specifying a clear and sufficient reason for doing so merely adds to the rage of Canadians who are frustrated, who are seeking a job to support their families, who are trying to keep their own businesses afloat, or who have had to shelve their own plans for developments or planned expansion because they simply do not have the money or the credit facilities to do so.
We would be much more willing to debate and pass this Bill if we knew what the money was needed for, when it is needed, how reliable the Minister's information is, and how much of this borrowing authority is requested because of the Government's mismanagement of public debt. We would also be much more confident if the Government's performance over the last few years had been more credible. But this Government has shown no inclination to reduce its expenditures, nor have we seen much benefit accruing from its high rate of spending for the past few years.
I would like to consider these two points in more detail. First of all, I would like to deal with the issue of credibility and accountability. The Government seeking this incredible borrowing authority has a track record of wildly inaccurate
forecasts. In his November, 1981 budget, Mr. MacEachen, then the Finance Minister, said the budget deficit would be $10.5 billion for 1982-83. Seven months later the unfortunate Mr. MacEachen revised that figure upwards to $19.6 billion. By October of the same year the budget deficit had risen still higher, to $23.6 billion and still climbing. Today the Minister indicates that the current forecast of the budget deficit for the current fiscal year will be in the order of $27 billion.
I would remind the House that this is the Government which thought its financial requirements for this year would be $6.6 billion. That figure again was adjusted upwards to $17.1 billion, and then $22.2 billion. Today the Government is asking for another $5 billion on top of these amounts.
Given that track record, how can we believe any figures the Government gives us now? How can we believe these figures when the Finance Minister indicates he will be back before this House, possibly as early as mid-summer, to seek even more borrowing authority?
It is now one o'clock, Mr. Speaker.

SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF BIOTECHNOLOGY CENTRE AT BROCK UNIVERSITY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, Canadians are proud of their country. Yet, when they think of their future, and read reports such as that recently released by the Conference Board of Canada predicting that the recession-ravaged Province of Ontario will suffer yet another loss of 25,000 jobs, putting that many more or that same number out or work, they wonder about their future as well as that of their country.

subtopic: SIZE OF GOVERNMENT DEFICIT
SIZE OF GOVERNMENT DEFICIT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) addressed this House earlier today on the borrowing requirements of the Government and briefly on the fiscal state of the nation. It was not a comforting scenario that he presented.
The projected Government deficit for the current year has exceeded $27 billion, an astronomical amount equivalent to $1,125 per person in Canada, or in excess of $3,000 per working Canadian. He announced that the 1983-84 federal Government expenditure framework is targeted at $88.9 billion, up almost 10 per cent over the current fiscal year. He also advised that revenues from corporate income tax, personal income tax, and petroleum and gas revenues have fallen substantially. This suggests a massive deficit for the 1983-84 fiscal year. He concluded that Canada has suffered a severe recession. Tax bases have fallen and unemployment has risen.
An economic crisis exists in the land, Madam Speaker, and a First Ministers' conference should be scheduled immediately to plan the road to recovery co-operatively.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, kick boxing is a form of martial art that is growing in popularity both in Canada and abroad. In kick boxing, both the hands and feet are used by the opponents to strike blows to the head of each when they meet in a ring to engage in competition.
What is unknown at this time, however, is how dangerous kick boxing can be. According to a spokesman for the Ontario Athletic Commission, there have been reports of severe facial injuries, including facial fractures, especially among youngsters who take up the sport. The impression of one Toronto neurologist, who is considered an expert on boxing injuries, is that kick boxing is a dangerous sport that should be looked at closely by the Ontario Commission.
Reports such as these have led the Ontario Government to ban kick boxing pending a government study into the possibility of serious head injuries to those participating in the sport. The Government of Ontario is to be complimented for taking the initiative in planning the study. I strongly urge the Department of National Health and Welfare and all provincial Ministers of Health to follow the example being set by the Ontario Government and initiate a full scale investigation into the sport of kick boxing, to co-ordinate their investigations and studies to control the serious body damage that this sport can generate, and to implement adequate regulations.

subtopic: APPLICATION TO DAIRY INDUSTRY
APPLICATION TO DAIRY INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have in my possession an internal memo from the Metric Commission in which a bureaucrat wrote and explained to a leading Canadian company president that metric conversion was a voluntary process. This will come as news to a great many Canadians.

February 17, 1983
The latest victim of the forced march toward metric is the dairy industry. The three-quart pouch packs and jugs will go metric next April, and the President of the Ontario Dairy Council estimates the new milk packages will probably cost about 40 cents more. The President of Dominion Dairies is on the record as stating "We're at a time when we should be avoiding increased costs. There is no doubt in my mind that increased costs will be passed on to consumers."
There are no indications that, once packaging new metric containers has been paid for, prices will be reduced. There are no benefits to be derived from the conversion of milk. To the contrary-it is the view of one of Canada's largest milk retailers that the industry and consumers are being "cheated and ripped off' by the unnecessary and expensive conversion costs. It is idiotic and unfair for a Government to put an unnecessary extra burden on the consumer at this time.

RENEWAL OF CALL FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF STANDING COMMITTEE

Madam Speaker, yesterday at a United Nations meeting on human rights in Geneva a report was delivered which indicated that two million people throughout the world have been executed in the last 15 years without trial, without appeal, and without lawyers. I should like to go on record today as indicating that the people who have been executed are human beings like you and me-men, women, people politically involved, people not politically involved, rich, poor-a cross section of humanity. Thirty-seven countries were listed as being involved in the event.
The person who made the statement to the United Nations Commission yesterday is Amos Wako, a Kenyan lawyer. He asked that the world community monitor this taking of human life. I think the House of Commons and the Government of Canada should be aware that this injustice is taking place around the world.
I would ask the Government to think seriously about forming an all-party standing committee on human rights to monitor, to publish, to condemn but, most important, to be a parliamentary group that would advise the Government about this abuse as it relates to the whole section of activity that takes place between countries.
