subtopic: FROST DAMAGE TO APPLE AND CHERRY ORCHARDS
FROST DAMAGE TO APPLE AND CHERRY ORCHARDS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on Thursday last in answer to a question by my colleague from York-Sunbury (Mr. Howie) regarding severe frost damage to Eastern Canada apple producers, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) indicated that he was aware of requests from both Ontario and Quebec. To use his words, "Quebec's damage is in the order of $62 million." Recently the Ontario Apple Marketing Commission went on record as requesting assistance for the apple growers in Eastern Ontario whose trees had been destroyed. My understanding is that the Eastern Ontario figure is close to the Quebec figure. The interesting part is that the better producing orchards were hardest hit.
In the few minutes I have I would like to add to the mix a problem which I have mentioned to the Minister many times in the past. It has to do with damage to sour cherry trees. One orchard in my riding has lost 8,000 trees as a result of the cumulative effect of frosts in 1980-1981. There is a market for this product, and the initial cost of replacing the trees is perhaps not beyond the reach of the owner. However, to pay the interest rate necessary to support such a loan for the five to seven years before the trees begin to bear fruit is just not possible. I want to use this time to urge the Minister of Agriculture as strongly as possible to take whatever action he can to help in this matter of great importance to area farmers.
February 17, 1983

subtopic: CREATION OF ADVOCACY AGENCIES URGED
CREATION OF ADVOCACY AGENCIES URGED
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, we all know about the situation of Pat Albert of Sudbury who was to have his unemployment insurance benefits cut off for a day because he had attended the funeral of his wife. It is not the first time this kind of injustice under the rule has taken place. Thank goodness the Government is bowing to public pressure and Pat Albert will not have this one day's benefit taken from him, and a 48-hour policy directive for funerals will be issued.
But the problem is bigger than this individual case. What we have here is a situation of David and Goliath. The unemployment insurance system is Goliath. It has the power of information, the knowledge of the Unemployment Insurance Act, the knowledge of the regulations and administrative directives, and the power to change those directives. Poor David is the individual Canadian unemployed for the first time who is faced with this administrative machinery. We have to give David a slingshot.
We have to create advocacy agencies for unemployment insurance claimants, funded by the Department of Justice. This would give professional knowledge to individual citizens when they have to deal with the unemployment insurance bureaucracy and would make it possible that, once in a while, the rules would work for the individual and not just for the bureaucracy. David could then slay Goliath once in a while.

subtopic: SILTING AT RUSTICO, P.E.I.-NEED FOR STUDY
SILTING AT RUSTICO, P.E.I.-NEED FOR STUDY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to address the very serious problem of silting in Rustico harbour, which is presently harming the fishing industry in Prince Edward Island. This problem could eventually affect the existence of the Village of North Rustico which depends heavily on the livelihood of its local fishermen.
The channel in Rustico has been dredged on a regular basis since 1966, and every year since 1976. The cost for dredging in 1981-1982 alone amounted to three-quarters of a million dollars. Little has been done to solve this problem, as dredging is merely a band-aid approach to a more serious problem. The dredge spent the best part of 1981 dredging the harbour channel. In 1982 the channel filled in again and was worse than the fishermen had seen in years.
The people of North Rustico wrote to the former Minister of Fisheries and Oceans, the Hon. Romeo LeBlanc, on the problem, but no action has been taken. I pursued the issue in the House on November 18, 1982, and I have written letters to both the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. De Bane) and to the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts) but have not received a reply from either Minister.
Oral Questions
This issue has been raised many times and we are expecting that action will be taken, as the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans has indicated the need for improved facilities in small craft harbours, as stated in the Kirby Task Force Report released today. In view of this I urge that a study be conducted of the Rustico harbour situation. Once this information is obtained, measures could be taken to rectify the problem on a permanent basis. This is a very serious problem on which immediate action should be taken.

speechtext:

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, Canadians are proud that we are governed by a parliamentary form of government. It is a form of government that has been with us for centuries, and a form of government whose first order of business is the raising of taxes and the responsible spending of taxpayers' money.
Today the Minister of Finance introduced a borrowing Bill which asks Parliament to approve the borrowing of $19 billion, with absolutely no explanation of how those funds would be expended.
Does the Minister of Finance not agree that to proceed at this time with this $19 billion borrowing authority would essentially violate the very tradition of parliamentary democracy?

subtopic: FINANCE
subsubtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY BILL C-143-ROLE OF PARLIAMENT

Madam Speaker, 1 would like to remind the Hon. Member that we began a debate this morning on this very Bill, and that the $19 billion is divided in two pieces, $5 billion to finance the operations of the Government between now and April 1, and $14 billion to meet interim financial requirements for the beginning of 198384.
This morning I spoke in the House for 45 minutes, giving the House all the relevant information on why this money was required and what it would be used for. 1 also indicated that, once the general debate has taken place on second reading, the Bill will go to committee, and that I would be very pleased to appear before the committee with my officials and go into all the details and questions which Hon. Members may want to raise concerning the use of those funds.
So, far from trying to get parliamentary approbation of expenditures without providing any figures or information, on the contrary, as I said, I took three-quarters of an hour this
morning to provide that information. Moreover, I will be happy to appear before the committee and go into even more details if my hon. friend wishes to have more information. This is what Parliament is all about, this floor in the House of Commons, and parliamentary committees. Indeed, this is how Parliament works in a democracy.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
subsubtopic: WEEKLY STATEMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as indicated yesterday, tomorrow is an Opposition day.

As far as the business of the Elouse for next week is concerned, Madam Speaker, on Monday we shall resume debate on the second reading stage of Bill C-139, to amend the Income Tax Act, and depending on the progress achieved that day, we could determine the order of business for Tuesday and Thursday. On Tuesday, we could very likely resume debate on Bill C-143, to provide the government with supplementary borrowing authority.
I have made some suggestions to the Progressive Conservative Party, and depending on their response, we might soon manage to complete the third reading stage of three urgently needed bills, first, Bill C-95, concerning events pools, the purpose of which is to provide large sums of money for the Olympic Games in Calgary; second Bill C-130, a very urgent one, to authorize continuing financial assistance to be provided to certain international financial institutions, and finally, Bill C-136, dealing with Small Business Investment Grants.
Should the Progressive Conservative Party's response concerning these three bills be favourable, we could complete on Tuesday the debate on the last stage, and on Thursday, we could consider the legislation on the borrowing authority, namely, Bill C-143.
What is sure, for the time being, is that we will deal on Monday with Bill C-139, and I will decide what will be the business for Tuesday on the basis of the Progressive Party House Leader's response and of course on the progress made with regard to the bill to amend the statute law relating to income tax.

subtopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I wonder if the Government House Leader would comment on a trend which seems to be taking place. The Government House Leader indicated yesterday, and again today, that he is going to allot tomorrow, which is a Friday, as an Opposition day. Tomorrow will be the fourth allotted day in this period. Of those four days, three of them have been on a Friday. In other words, a short day.
I am sure that the Government House Leader is aware that, by allotting short days, the Government is cutting down on the debating time which is allowed to the Opposition. If in fact all of the allotted days were to be Fridays, a total of 25 hours, or 20 per cent of the debating time, would be taken away by the Government. What we really have, Madam Speaker, is closure by allotment. I ask the Government House Leader to assure us that, in allotting the rest of those days, a fairer treatment will be given to the Opposition in order that we can deal with these matters that way, rather than a long debate on a question of privilege.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
subsubtopic: WEEKLY STATEMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, since we started our parliamentary reform experiment, we have had no more short days, because now, there is no private members' hour on Friday, and thus Fridays are much longer now than they used to be. Furthermore, I can assure the Hon. Member that we shall not use the kind of tricks they like to use on days set aside for Government Orders or shorten Opposition days by letting the bells ring indefinitely, nor do we intend to indulge in dilatory tactics to prevent them from considering private member's business.
That being said, I am certainly not going to schedule Opposition days on Friday as a matter of course. The schedule will of course depend on the progress of the business of the House and consideration by the House of certain Bills. I can assure the Hon. Member that I shall seriously consider his suggestion with respect to future Opposition days. However, I would like to point out that if we look at the time spent on the business of Parliament on a given day, on average, the House spends far more time on Opposition days, even on Fridays, compared to the amount of time spent on Government business on other days of the week, and that is due to the dilatory tactics used by the Opposition party in recent weeks.

That is exactly the point which I was making to the House and to the Government House Leader.

Madam Speaker, the answer is as follows.

The Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development requested that a formal public review of this proposal be undertaken by an Environmental Assessment Panel. The Minister of the Environment appointed a Panel in January, 1981 to undertake this task. The Panel issued guidelines for the preparation of an environmental impact statement to the Band in March, 1981. Since that time the Band and the City of Winnipeg have held discussions in an attempt to overcome concerns related to the proposed development. A completion date therefore cannot be determined at present, (c) Yes, the review will primarily focus on the potential effects of the proposed development on water quality and will examine subjects listed in question 1 (c). subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 (NO. 3) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Lalonde that Bill C-143, to provide supplementary borrowing authority, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 (NO. 3) MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the recess 1 was describing how the Government is seeking to borrow an unprecedented amount of money to pay unspecified bills for programs not yet clearly identified. I explained how this huge borrowing represents a deferred tax on taxpayers in the future and how it constrains the action of the present and future Governments. 1 also detailed how the Government's record of forecasting has been wildly inaccurate and how in this Bill the Government fails to address the real problems in the economy, the deep, structural shifts which have closed our plants, our mills and our mines and which cloud the future of the unemployed in Canada, particularly the young.
I said we would be much more willing to debate and pass this Bill if we knew what the money was needed for, when it is needed and how reliable the Minister's information is and that we would be much more confident if the Government's performance over the last few years had been more credible.
I should like to continue by asking how the Government feels that it can properly and responsibly ask Parliament to approve this borrowing when it has refused to provide economic and fiscal projections beyond the current year in the last two budgets? How can the Minister seek this kind of spending authority when he refuses to answer any of our questions? Why should we approve this Bill when the Government is vague about the uses to which it will be put and when the Minister can give us no idea about the projected size of the deficit in the next fiscal year? What will next year's deficit be? The idea of picking a number between S20 billion and $30 billion is not the sort of game that Parliament should be asked to play.
Clearly, the Government is withholding information from Parliament. It claims it needs this additional money because revenues have fallen due to the recession and because of the additional cost of servicing the public debt, which, of course, represents interest charges on money borrowed in the past. But in fact, the Minister is cooking the books again in his statement to the House today. He attempts to justify his horrendously increasing deficit by arguing that substantial reductions in the deficit were achieved in three previous fiscal years.
This morning the Minister argued that the Government's financial requirements dropped from a level equivalent to 4.8 per cent of GNP in 1978-79 to only 2.5 per cent of GNP in 1981-82. He failed to note that, using his own figures, the Government's financial requirements for the current fiscal year of $26.1 billion will amount to 7.5 per cent of nominal
Borrowing Authority
GNP, an increase of 200 per cent on a year-over-year basis. That is cooking the books by anyone's definition, Mr. Speaker.
The Minister also ignores the fact that, in terms of revenue, we must expect that the worst is yet to come because of the time lag in collecting revenue. We would not expect the full impact of the decline in economic activity and Government revenues until later this year when companies and individuals file their tax returns and pay any taxes due on their activities during the past year.
So much for the Government's credibility. Let us look at its performance now. As I said earlier, we would be more willing to approve this Bill if the Government's performance in managing the economy were better. Unfortunately, its performance has been abysmal. It has shown no signs of moderating its expenditures, nor has its chronically high rate of spending been of benefit to the economy, as the two million unemployed will testify.
It is particularly ironic that this request for borrowing $19 billion comes on the eve of the anniversary of the Government's election in 1980. At that time the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said this:
We will hold the line on Government expenditure growth to under the rate of G.N.P.-
The deficit will be reduced in a phased and orderly fashion ... any new expenditure programs to meet the evolving needs and requirements of Canadians will be financed by reallocating existing expenditures or by increases in revenue.
In reality, since 1980 the Government has increased its spending at twice the rate of GNP, adjusted for inflation. Since 1980, the deficit has more than doubled. So much for the promises of the Prime Minister.
Since the Government took office in February, 1980, Government spending has increased by 66 per cent compared with an increase in the CPI of 38 per cent and compared to nominal GNP growth of 30 per cent. Clearly, the Prime Minister and the Government have been unable to come close to keeping his election promises.
As a matter of fact, it is interesting to look at the impact of Government spending and its relationship to the unemployment figures. In 1970-71 when the deficit was around $370 million, the unemployment rate was 5.7 per cent; in 1975-76 when the deficit was $5.4 billion, the unemployment rate was nearly 7 per cent. But today when the deficit is up to $26 billion, the unemployment rate is well over 12 per cent. The only conclusion is that the more the Government borrows, the higher the rate of unemployment.
This record is not confined to the present Minister of Finance and his unhappy predecessor; it has continued through the record of Finance Ministers of Liberal persuasion in the past. When John Turner was Finance Minister, inflation doubled from less than 5 per cent to more than 10 per cent. When Donald Macdonald was Finance Minister, unemployment rose from 7 per cent to 8 per cent and the deficit increased from nearly $5 billion to more than $8 billion. This kind of legacy, of course, has been outlined by the Auditor General in his reports.

February 17, 1983
Borrowing Authority
We must look at this record of deficits, and of irresponsible borrowing in light of the current situation when we have the twin evils of a recessionary economy aggravated by Government mismanagement. For Canada as a whole our real GNP fell by 1 per cent in the third quarter of 1982 which is the fifth consecutive quarter of decline. Real GNP has now fallen by 6.9 per cent since the second quarter of 1981. In the third quarter of 1982 manufacturing was operating at only 68 per cent of capacity, which is the lowest level since records were first kept in 1961. Canada needs 210,000 housing units each year to meet demand. In 1982 only 125,000 units were built.
According to the OECD, Canada's economic decline in 1982 was the worst of any of the 24 members of the OECD. According to the September 1982 issue of Euromoney, the over-all performance of the Canadian economy since 1974 ranks us fortieth in the world.
Over the past few years, our industrial productivity has been rising at the slowest rate of any major industrial nation. Of course, the impact on some of the Provinces, such as my home Province of British Columbia, has been very great. In B.C. the people are exhausting their unemployment insurance benefits at the rate of 9,000 per month. Welfare cases in the Province have jumped by more than 51 per cent since last year. Business bankruptcies in B.C. last year have more than doubled.
This is a dreary record created in part by a dishonest Government which augurs a dismal future for Canadians, who are paying the costs and will pay the costs for years to come. The Government's billowing debt threatens to throttle the fragile recovery which may emerge later this year.
The current Conference Board forecast shows a slow recovery from the recession starting this year with a modest growth in GNP, improving in 1984, but the unemployment rate is still expected to stay well above double-digit numbers. The cruellest impact of the Government's failure to develop the promise of Canada is evidenced by the rising numbers of Canadians who have lost their jobs.
When we look at alternative policies, Mr. Speaker, we have to look at the policies put forward by the NDP. I was amused this morning to note that the NDP finance critic noted his concern about the deficit. He said that he was deeply concerned about the size of the deficit. That is not what he has been saying. In a recent letter to The Globe and Mail, the finance critic for the NDP wrote:
in the reality of today, not all Government deficit is wrong ... clearly, the Government has a responsibility to borrow in order to stimulate the economy at a critical time such as now.
The NDP has also proposed economic policies which include emphasis on Government planning and increasing the corporate tax rate. In essence, the NDP is saying that more state planning is good for Canada. But this philosophy requires the Government to pick the winners and losers in the economic system. It is the same kind of thinking that spawned the National Energy Program and the 1981 MacEachen budget, which have proved to be such disasters.
We believe in the Conservative Party that these choices should be left to the marketplace. Our position is quite clear on this. We feel the only way to achieve a sustained and solid recovery is to restore stability to the Canadian economy. But stability can only emerge in a favourable climate or environment created within the framework of clearly defined Government policies. This environment must encourage the inflow of capital from other countries to augment Canada's own scarce capital resources and must encourage Canadians to conserve and expand our own capital base. Without such incentives, Canadians will not be able to create the job opportunities which are required before they can go back to work. Those who are lucky enough to be employed will not spend their hard-earned dollars on consumer purchases if they find themselves worried about their job situation. I am sorry that the Minister for Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro) finds that so amusing.
Similarly, we need to assist small businesses in particular to keep operating by helping them to husband their cash flow. Over and over again I am told by small-businessmen that they need such assistance as John Crosbie's Small Business Development Bond, which was a cash flow bond which enabled them to keep operating.
Over and over again I am told that small-businessmen need financial instruments to enable them to plan ahead, that they need simpler taxation measures.
Over and over again I am told by small-businessmen that the accounting costs of calculating tax advantages under the existing mish-mash of small business regulations and registration far exceeds any financial advantage to them.
For both large and small companies the need to improve their liquidity is very great, one of the biggest concerns in this country.
Over and over again 1 am told we need training programs that are not the inflexible training programs devised by this Government which limits the businessman's opportunity to use the people employed. We might consider specific incentives, such as a graduated capital gains tax or training incentives which account for management's time in training. Instead of positive, specific programs we have before us only borrowing Bills, the current one for $19 billion.
What is $19 billion? I would like to refer to this morning's The Globe and Mail. The editorial column has an assessment of what $19 billion is. Let me put it on the record:
What's $19 billion? This is how much it is. It is the size of the federal Government's entire budget in 1973-74: revenues were $19.3 billion that year, expenditures $20.04 billion. It is the size of the entire net debt of the country, the accumulated over all deficit since Confederation, as recently as 1974-75-
Indeed, the ever-increasing size of Liberal Government deficits since the midseventies has brought us to the point where, not our debt but the mere interest payments on our debt have become greater than total budgetary expenditures were when Pierre Trudeau came to power.
That is $19 billion, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to deal with a problem which is of major concern in my constituency, a problem which I have been facing for several weeks involving the whole question of unemployment in Canada as well as the bill now under consideration.
We know that a supplementary authority bill was introduced as a possible solution but, because of the economic slowdown and the resulting decrease in fiscal revenue and increase in unemployment insurance or welfare payments, the Liberal government is in my view acting as a responsible and more importantly as a reliable government by providing the people of Quebec with at least the basic necessities of life.
I would like to draw the attention of the House to a problem which was raised during the debate on Bill S-31 dealing specifically with investments by the Caisse de depot et placement du Quebec into companies involved in interprovincial transportation.
However, Mr. Speaker, I believe the principle which was applied to the Caisse de depot should be extended in practice. In my constituency, a building material plant owned by Domtar has just closed down and I disagree with this decision which put laid-off employees on unemployment insurance even though the plant still lead an operating capacity. Mr. Speaker, Domtar was acquired by the Caisse de depot, which now owns 46 percent of all shares in the company. Through the appointment of nine members on the board of directors and the chairmanship of Mr. Yves Pratte, a former constitutional advisor to the Quebec government the Caisse de depot has been able to gain full control of Domtar. Mr. Speaker, when a Quebec institution such as the Caisse de depot, whose responsibility it is to invest the pension funds of workers has its own staff on unemployment insurance, I believe there is ground for concern, and I want to thank the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) for getting the money he needs through this borrowing bill; however, I am still concerned by Domtar's decision.
Borrowing Authority
This company decided to close down its Quebec plant in the middle of its negotiations with its employees, after only 11 meetings. The workers had graciously accepted the 6 and 5 federal program and during the negotiations on the normative clauses, they were told they were now without a job. Mr. Speaker, 21 of these workers had served at least 30 years, a dozen had been working for the company for 20 years or more and twelve for over ten years, which means most of these workers now find themselves on unemployment insurance at 45, 50 or 55 years of age with little chance of finding another job because of the compounding effect of a bad economic situation and a dwindling labour market. Consequently, unskilled labourers or plant workers without specific technical training will have either to face a difficult retraining period to get back into the labour market or go on welfare when their unemployment insurance has run out. And in my view this is a palliative that seems to be the only way out at this point and that 1 cannot approve.
I am asking that corporation a question for the simple reason that their operations as a Quebec-based multinational company owned by Quebecers, through the Caisse de Depot, in other words the pension fund of those very workers, are being transferred to Ontario. This I consider an arbitrary decision, Mr. Speaker. Economic recovery is around the corner, interest rates are lower, construction is about to resume in Quebec, and this company manufactures gypsum boards that have always been of high quality, that have been part of the Eastern market. Those gypsum boards made in Montreal, in the riding of Mercier, were sold not only in Quebec, but also in the Maritimes and in New York state. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, the fact that we are compelled at this point to borrow in order to finance such a move by a company owned by Quebecers and financed by the Caisse de Depot, whose workers will have to live off unemployment benefits, and the fact that we are compelled to borrow while such high-handed decisions are being taken, cause me to rise and ask questions from a corporation which I regard as irresponsible.
If a Government such as ours is forced at this point in time to go out and get some money either by way of borrowing or through this country's consolidated revenue-although currently we are short of revenues due to the increased number of people that are drawing unemployment insurance benefits-1 feel they should be concerned with the lack of social awareness of some corporations. We have a federal work-sharing program that not only has helped most people to save their jobs but also is most compassionate by its very nature. Admittedly, Mr. Speaker, it must be financed through contributions obtained from the Unemployment Insurance Fund. It provides for two things: first, companies are allowed to keep their qualified workers, and second, those workers are assured of keeping their morale high and the work skills they have developed while waiting for an economic recovery.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I feel that everyone has to make a contribution, and private enterprise also must do its share. Under the current conditions, the private business sector is controlled by the Quebec government. The workers went to see

Mr. Parizeau, who simply told them he was not getting involved. He only gets involved when it suits him. Apparently, the matter lies on Mr. Biron's and Mr. Landry's desks, and finally on the desks of all Quebec ministers and former ministers. They are unable to deal with the matter of a company with 90 employees. Some may say that 90 employees drawing unemployment benefits is not a major problem. But we must remember that decisions like those are made and repeated many times, and especially by companies such as this one who should be aware of their social responsibilities.
Mr. Speaker, in Quebec in 1976, the unemployment rate was less than 10 per cent. It has now gone up to 15 per cent or more, and we have an incredible number of people on the welfare rolls. Through its programs, the Federal Government is helping many Quebec families but it cannot be said that any substantial assistance has been received from the provincial authorities. In the process of taking controlling interest in corporations such as Domtar, the provincial authorities are forgetting that the workers concerned have in fact worked most of their lives. After a while, their productivity goes down, and they are no longer as young as they were. As a result of collective agreements and seniority and the number of weeks of leave to which they are entitled, they have become to expensive to "keep up", and so they are treated like obsolete equipment that can be simply got rid of, and put on unemployment insurance.
Mr. Speaker, I think that even if our Government is discharging its responsibilities through the kind of borrowing measures the House is considering today, it is not up to the Federal Government alone to bear this burden. On the other hand, I think that this borrowing measure will help us to uphold the principles supported by a Liberal Government, namely, the universality of programs such as Family Allowances and Old Age Security. Mr. Speaker, anyone who is familiar with the financial administration of the Federal Government will realize that these programs require very substantial funds. I feel, however, that in a recession, at a time of great financial difficulty, we must not forget those people who would otherwise become the victims of the situation as has happened in the United States, as a result of the conservative policies of the Reagan Government, which decided to resolve its economic problems by cutting social programs.
Furthermore, I think that a responsible government, like the Liberal Government, understands where its responsibilities lie and has the requisite compassion for these people who are having to face such difficult times. Mr. Speaker, as Canadians, we have no choice but to draw from our national wealth. Economic recovery is imminent. Mr. Speaker, at the present time, we have both the capability and the need to borrow. I believe that people who will be receiving money from the Federal Government which is now experiencing a drop in revenue and of course, an increase in payments, I believe that
these people will now be able to bridge the gap between economic recovery and the present recession.
Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, to get back to the situation in my riding, at Domtar, I urgently request the officials of that company and the federal authorities to drop their adjustment committee and to use programs such as the time-sharing agreement. There is still time to get this plant operating again. There is still time to manufacture gypsum board in Montreal, because, and the Minister's statistics are eloquent, construction is starting up again across Canada, and especially in Quebec. I must say that my riding is particularly well-suited to providing the kind of residential construction we all need.
Mr. Speaker, I have a riding that is developing steadily, with a growing population. We have land available and all the programs and infrastructures necessary to get ahead. We have the demand, and then we have a company that is simply shutting down.
Mr. Speaker, I am merely repeating what the workers have told me, workers I represent in the House of Commons. I am therefore asking the company and the Government of Quebec to act responsibly as the Federal Government has done, in these difficult times, and to enable these workers to keep their jobs.
Mr. Speaker, finally, I would like to point out that we must realize that the situation is very serious. Certainly, we are borrowing funds to help a group of people who need help, but in Quebec, the situation is almost hopeless as far as the Charter of Rights is concerned. The Province of Quebec is now going through difficult and sad times, and I simply want to appeal to the solidarity of the people of Montreal-Mercier and of all Quebecers. It is not a problem between English- and French-speaking Canadians, it is not a problem between the rich and the poor, it is not a question of knowing who will get what from the Federal or the Provincial Government. No, it is a problem of solidarity, of mutual respect, and of our common future.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope the Hon. Member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) did not imply that if one were not an income tax expert, one would automatically be a second-class Parliamentarian. I submit that if we are to be truly representative of the Canadian people, it is not necessary to be an income tax expert. I would say that it is very necessary to understand people, to understand their needs and aspirations and, more than anything, to have what is regularly known as a certain amount of common sense. Unfortunately, it is not as common as its name would imply. One would wish at times we had more of it, even in this august Chamber.
Dealing with the borrowing authority Bill, the first point to be made is that the need for the Bill should not come as a surprise to anybody. 1 do not think I have heard anyone say that they are surprised. Perhaps they were alarmed or overwhelmed, and many other words could be used depending on which side of the House you speak from. They may have been alarmed at the amount.
I believe the first point to be made is that no one was really surprised that the Government needed to borrow money to tide it over to the end of this fiscal year. Why? Let us look at it in a common sense way which, as I have already said, is unfortunately not common enough. We have to look first at the global situation. Everyone who has read a newspaper, watched TV or listened to a radio has witnessed a recession, the magnitude of which we have not seen since the early 1930s, and it has been global. We have witnessed high unemployment, record levels of unemployment, in all the industrialized countries. We have witnessed tremendous uncertainty among OPEC countries. We still have that uncertainty with us. Perhaps another week or so will give us a better picture of how we are going to project our own budget for the coming year. We cannot be immune to these situations which occur in other countries. They do affect us. At home we have had two drastically high unemployment periods, which means not only human suffering and misery but, more practically, record levels of payment out of the Unemployment Insurance Fund.
There are those of us, and I count myself among them, who thank God that we have an unemployment insurance plan which gives a safety net to those people who, through no fault of their own, lose their jobs. We do have an Unemployment Insurance Fund but it has been depleted. Many of our constituents have even depleted what benefits they were getting from the Unemployment Insurance Fund and have had to go
on municipal welfare or, worse still, provincial welfare, because that means a longer term. Obviously, the coffers have been depleted because fewer people have been working, because the oil prices have not risen as one year ago it seemed they would rise. The Government receives less revenue. High interest rates, which are coming down now, were also added to the national debt. We had to pay more money to service the national debt. But these things are improving, Mr. Speaker. The global situation now is much healthier than it was even a few short weeks ago. We now have rapidly falling interest rates, as a result of which the Government's debt will be more easily borne by Canadian taxpayers. Hopefully, interest rates will continue to go down. The economic indices are good. Things are going to improve.
However, let me say again, no thoughtful Canadian should be surprised at this stage that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) needs more money to tide him over to the end of the fiscal year. No one should be surprised at that, nor can anyone blame him. However, once we have reached the end of the fiscal year, the Minister has already spoken about interim financing toward June. What is he going to do with that money? That is what I would like to direct my remarks to, Mr. Speaker. It is the main theme of my presentation today in the House. What is the Minister going to do with that money? How is it that he cannot wait until later, after the budget, to get money in order to put forward his programs? I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the very fact that the budget has not been brought down, nor will it be for another few weeks, at least, explains in part why the Minister must have the authority to borrow money now and not when it is too late. Let me explain. We have read in today's press that the budget will probably be brought down sometime in April. No one knows the exact date, not even the Minister of Finance himself. In that budget the Minister will announce specific projects. We in this Chamber know how long legislation takes, how long debate takes. We should be the first to understand the lead time which will be necessary in order for these programs to be implemented.
Let me focus my remarks on my particular wishes for the programs of the future. I refer to the youth constituency, Mr. Speaker, because irrespective of the upturn in the economy which will come, irrespective of the tremendous growth which will come, we have to be realistic and understand that when employers start re-hiring, they will re-hire the skilled and trained workers. The youth component will be very, very low on the totem pole. The youth are the ones who will be hired last and, unfortunately, will be the first fired. 1 do not believe, being realistic, that the private sector will turn its attention in the immediate future to the youth of this country. The Government must look after the youth component. They are our future. The Government will need money now before it can even start formulating the programs for our youth. What kind of programs am I suggesting? First of all, I believe that in discussing youth needs we should be very careful, Mr. Speaker, not to generalize. We women would be very upset if people
February 17, 1983

generalized about our aspirations and needs. The men would also resent any kind of generalization. We cannot generalize about youth. There are various categories with various needs, just as with the adult constituency.
In order to make our approach simpler, I believe we, as legislators, and, hopefully, the public, should have at least three broad categories for youth who this summer, just a few weeks from now, will desperately need our hlep. In the first category, very broadly, are the youth who have finished their formal education. They have left school. They have a certain amount of formal education but not very much practical experience. They will need full-time jobs. The proposal which grew from this side of the Flouse, Mr. Speaker, refers primarily to that category. It is not, and I repeat, it is not a panacea for all the ills of Canadian youth, for all the needs of Canadian youth, but it is at least a firm proposal by which a certain number of Canadian youth, who so wish, will be absorbed for a short period of time into the Armed Forces. That is a full-time job.
The second category of youth, I would submit, is the university students who will be coming out of school, perhaps, as soon as May, just a few months from now. Many of these young people have stayed in university longer than they originally planned to do at the beginning. Perhaps some of them would have been happy with just a simple BA, but now because of the economic situation they have fears that they will not get a job, and those fears are well founded. They cannot get a job now in our society as it is. Therefore, they have chosen to stay in university, perhaps at some financial sacrifice to themselves and to their families. I am sure society as a whole will benefit from this in the long run because the future generation will be more educated than the preceding one. However, we must help those university students to continue to pay for their tuition by finding them summer jobs. As I said before, I doubt very much that the private sector can supply jobs in the numbers needed for these students. But I hope any jobs we do find them will be jobs that will help them in their career aspirations, not just make-work jobs, but jobs which would give them on-the-job experience they will need when they eventually go into the private sector and ask for work.
1 would suggest, therefore, that perhaps the universities, the laboratories, could be given extra grants in order to hire the students who need summer jobs and, therefore, give them the practical expertise during the summer which they are learning in theory during the winter months. It is only a suggestion, I do not know if it will be accepted.
The other category is the high school students. Here again we now know that enrolment last year was much higher all over the country than it has been for many years. Why? Again, the kids decided to stay at school rather than go on unemployment insurance or face a job market where there were no jobs for them. Here again there was a financial
Borrowing Authority
sacrifice particularly on the part of those students' families. We have to help them. These students, in their hundreds, will be coming into the summer job market, perhaps in the middle or at end of June. What is going to happen to them? I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that it would be unwise, to say the least, perhaps irresponsible, on the part of Government to even place advertisements, such as it did in today's newspapers, offering them summer jobs if the Government itself is not sure it would have the means of providing for the payment of those programs. I suggest that is the kind of thing the Minister of Finance meant this morning when he said that our job was to provide for the needs of those who need help most.
In my submission, we have to be prepared in the coming months to face the tremendous number of young people who are going to be turning not to the private sector but to all of us in this Chamber and begging for help. I do not think they need to beg. We should not make them do so. We should be preparing them now and saying "Look, there is hope".
Of course, Mr. Speaker, it is embarrassing for any Government to have to ask permission to borrow money. But do you not think it would be morally reprehensible if we were not to ask for that money to spend it on worth-while programs such as those I just mentioned? I believe, Mr. Speaker, that our first duty is to the people of Canada, to help them when they need help most, when there is no one else to do it for them. Therefore, I would say yes, we are facing a deficit. No one is very comfortable about it, but we are using the money for worth-while purposes, and I think that Canada's youth will thank us for it in the end.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, presentation of the Bill before us which seeks authority to borrow a substantial amount of money, is a very common procedure in the House of Commons. It is almost a knee-jerk reaction in which we find the House being presented with a blank cheque. Sometimes the Government makes certain gestures toward the provision of information about the need for borrowing. In each case that we have been faced with, the amounts are larger and larger while the information is scarcer and scarcer each time the Bill comes before us.
I recall that when the last Bill was before us we engaged in a very intensive debate about the matter. At that time the other Party with whom we share the Opposition benches informed the Canadian people that they had won a great victory by not signing the blank cheque right away. Eventually, however, they did sign half the cheque, and after a couple of days of debate they signed the last half of the cheque.
What we have now is a situation where debate in the House of Commons winds up being largely a matter of knee-jerk reaction. Many Members of the House believe that this is a very substantial amount of money to be borrowed and that certainly, prior to giving support in principle at second reading stage, it would be better if we were to refer the question of borrowing to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs. I hope that this amendment will be accepted by the majority of Members in the House.
There have been allusions to the causes of the economic dilemma that faces us today. I think it is fairly clear why the Government has to borrow. We are in a very severe recession in which Government revenues have definitely dropped, Government programs have been strained to the nth degree in an attempt to support individuals in difficult times. These programs have not been doing a great job in supporting those individuals, given the unemployment figures, bankruptcy figures, the erosion of the social institutions mentioned by the previous speaker such as the university community and technical schools which are all faced with very severe cutbacks in teaching staff, increase in pupil-teacher ratios, class size and lack of material.
Let me just digress for a moment. I would point out that a Dean of an Engineering Faculty to whom I was speaking, responsible at the time for instruction of post-graduate students in electrical engineering, told me that recently his class sizes had risen to the point where he found it very difficult to teach. He was in a fairly lucky position with tenure and a fairly reasonable salary. He found himself well above the other

February 17, 1983
Borrowing Authority
members of the faculty, especially the new ones, in terms of security and salary. At the time the university was increasing class sizes dramatically. The university was refusing to provide appropriate equipment to keep its post-graduate students on the leading edge of technology which would enable them to leave as competent, trained engineers. The junior faculty was being siphoned off quickly into industry where the benefits and salaries were much higher and where the opportunities to improve and develop their professional capacity was much greater. Largely through federal Government and provincial Governments' restraint activities the university faculties were being gutted. Once we have caused harm to the students it will have a life-long effect on those individuals. If we gut our universities now it will be a decade or more before they can recover.
The motion before us this afternoon proposes that we take a serious look at the implications of this borrowing Bill. Maybe we can determine some of the directions in which we should be moving to spend that money when we determine what amount of money is appropriate. There is an enormous failure on the part of the Government today. There is enormous incompetence on the part of the Government today. No one argues that we have not been drawn into a deep world-wide recession, from which Canada cannot be excluded. But unfortunately the negative, social and economic impacts on this country have been compounded by an incompetent Liberal Government.
Let me outline one example of the complete incompetence of this Government as it relates to the National Energy Program. In 1980, during the election, the subject of energy and the cost of energy was widely talked about. We heard how we were going to develop security of supply and how we were going to be protected from high price energy. These were made the topics of the election campaign. Certain commitments were made by this Liberal Government on those topics. Basically, Government revenues were to be enhanced, the price of fuel was going to be controlled and ultimately the megaprojects would be the economic salvation of this country. All of that was embodied in what was called the National Energy Program in 1980. We heard the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde), who was then the Minister of Energy, making firm commitments in the House of Commons about the benefits that Canadians would receive. We heard that the megaprojects would put us back to work. The NEP would be the engine which fuelled the economy, supported other businesses, created employment and took away regional disparity. The promises went on and on. The National Energy Program was also to be the salvation of what had been in the past incompetent Liberal Governments. These Liberal Governments wound up with enormous deficits and eroded the strength of Government programs. Ultimately, the National Energy Program was to be an enormous cash grab by the federal Government shared with the Provinces and the producing companies, which would solve all our economic problems. The revenue figure used by the Government was $65 billion. It is very difficult to get one's head around that amount of money. It certainly pales the deficit.
We also talked about the possibility of Atlantic Canada becoming financially secure, energy self-sufficient and spinning off the results of industrial and economic development into the twenty-first century. We were told that all this would create opportunities in areas of the country that traditionally had great difficulties.
It was not too long after that that Bill C-48, the legislative vehicle that implemented the National Energy policy, was rammed through this House by closure. It was rammed through committee. It was a very difficult and complicated piece of legislation. The Minister told us, "We do not want to spell out the details. We want you, legislators, to give me, the Minister of Energy, discretionary power," and the amount of discretion in that Bill was enormous. We saw the Government ram that legislation through the House. It put the National Energy Program into place. It was hardly implemented when its collapse became evident to most people.
Ultimately, we wound up in 1982 with what was called the National Energy Program Update. It became obvious that the original projections, the megaprojects, had collapsed. That engine to fire the economy to assist us in recovery from recession, collapsed because of the incompetence of the Government.
The Government had made a quick snatch at revenue in the amount of $65 billion. But in the 1982 Energy Update it changed its projections. The projections became an amount between $25 billion and $30 billion. The Government wound up again confounded with problems of assistance to regional developments because of the collapse of particular projects or the delaying of them.
Again, we come to face what we have today, a request to borrow $19 billion. One of the reasons we are faced with this borrowing, the particular depth of recession and the harm caused by it, is the incompetence of the Government. What is that incompetence? The Government took a terrible risk. It risked the industrial and economic future of this country in one economic sector. The Government threw the dice on one particular sector, that of energy. The Government made a snatch at a goose it thought was going to lay a golden egg. But eventually it found there was nothing there. Instead, the Government placed Canadians and the whole economy of our nation in the hands of OPEC, a cartel which was controlling the world supply of oil and its price. Unfortunately for the Government of Canada, the OPEC cartel collapsed. OPEC was not a platform upon which this Government could build a sound economy in Canada. But that is very traditional with the Liberals. Liberal Governments in this country have looked for the economic salvation of Canada in the export of raw, unprocessed natural resources. At one time it was coal and unprocessed base metals that were being shipped to the Japanese, and other world markets. In the future it looks as though we may be shipping unprocessed forest products to the United States. The same will be true of the export of raw energy resources, natural gas and oil. We talked about 900 years of natural gas and 900 years of oil around a decade ago. Suddenly that wheel turned back and Canada has a shortage of supply. But now we are being told again that we have a very heavy surplus. Believe
February 17, 1983

me, Mr. Speaker, we have been put through this exercise one too many times.
It is interesting to note that the National Energy Program collapsed. This was the industrial sell-out for raw materials in Canada. The Update has collapsed. The most recent events in the collapse of the National Energy Program Update were seen in the total collapse of the megaprojects. There are no jobs to be created in that area nor any stimulus for Canadian business.
We look to the collapse of the Canada-Newfoundland Energy Agreement. We can take no comfort in the fact that the Appeal Court of Newfoundland has ruled in favour of the the federal Government of Canada. At some point in time officials of this federal Government will have to sit down with officials of the Province of Newfoundland, play fair ball and bargain in good faith. Unless this Government is prepared to give the Government of Newfoundland a fair and even partnership in the development of that resource, we will see the same kinds of economic problems emerge. Fairness was preached about so much in the National Energy Program. That fairness will be put off for decades. The Government of Newfoundland simply asks for an opportunity to manage that resource in such a way that a portion of the $100 billion projected from Hibernia will stay in Newfoundland. But the only way that can occur is if the people of Newfoundland have some say in the management, the development and the opportunity to pace that development so that industries in Newfoundland and Atlantic Canada are to share in the benefits of resource development.
History is very clear. What happened to the majority of jobs created by the North Sea oil? They wound up in the United States. The collapse of the megaprojects is one thing. It is time the federal Government came back to the table with Newfoundland, put aside the matter of who owns the resource and looked at how we as Canadians will share the benefits, thus providing an opportunity for the people of Newfoundland and Atlantic Canada to pull themselves out of economic dilemmas they have faced for so much of their history. It could also provide an industrial and an economic base that will support them after the oil is gone.
We look at the collapse of revenue. The National Energy Program Update dealt with certain recovery measures that were meant to get the federal Government into an acceptable revenue position. Perhaps we could look here for some of the funds for programs for young people that the previous speaker spoke of, as well as for some programs for the unemployed that would help get some economic initiatives rekindled.
Unfortunately, that Update to the National Energy Program has collapsed again. We have seen the price of energy on the international market fall to the point where oil will likely replace natural gas. The Government is trying to sell enormous volumes of natural gas. The National Energy Board provided for the sale of enormous volumes of natural gas into the United
Borrowing Authority
States. In order to stick to the Government's promise to keep the domestic price of gas at 65 per cent of the equivalent price of oil, the Government has dropped $300 million in revenue. From this type of poor planning we have seen a drop in projected revenues from $65 billion to $30 billion on the first update. We have seen a drop of $300 million in natural gas earnings alone. There has been a tremendous loss in projected revenues ever since the National Energy Program Update in 1982. This brings us back to the collapse of the energy projects and the collapse of the Canada-Newfoundland energy agreement. Now we have the collapse of the revenue projections.
We talked a great deal about fairness throughout both of those phoney energy policy reports. There were errors in Government judgment in regard to the economic and industrial recovery for Canada.
As recently as last Thursday, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Chretien) stated in Vancouver that one of the Government's main commitments was to build pipelines to allow the people of Atlantic Canada to capitalize on natural gas as an alternative energy source to oil and to allow the people of Vancouver Island to have natural gas as an alternative. There are no developed alternatives to oil on Vancouver Island at present. There was a commitment of $150 million to build that pipeline and pay the conversion costs on Vancouver Island. Last Thursday, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources appeared to have scrapped that plan. I and many Canadians would appreciate it, in a spirit of fair play, hearing from Minister in the House for the sake of the people of Vancouver Island whether that gas pipeline is to go ahead. He indicated that it would not because a review of the costs proved them to be exorbitant.
The National Energy Board came out with a proposal about a week and a half ago to increase the export of natural gas primarily to the United States market. It represents an enormous increase in volume. I believe the rationale behind that decision is unacceptable. There are certainly problems with it. But the federal Government has left itself open to blackmail from the industry which tells the Government to either sell the gas or they will shut down. On the other hand, the Americans are pushing us by saying they will not take our gas unless the Government drives down the prices, substantially. We are faced with the prospect of Canadians paying billions in incentives to drill for gas. The companies pay about six cents, and the Canadian taxpayer pays about 94 cents on the dollar for the risk of exploring for that new and expensive oil and gas. Yet the Government is prepared to sell enormous volumes of cheaper gas to the American market which cannot even absorb that volume. Canadians will find themselves further behind the eight-ball as a result of paying these enormous incentive grants, while the Government's revenues from energy are greatly reduced on sales of a very valuable resource which the Government is prepared to give to the United States at sale prices.
Let us consider the economic logic of this plan in which the Americans end up with cheap energy to produce cheaper goods

that will compete with our high priced goods in a very competitive world market. The economic logic behind the cheap gas export fails completely. The failed logic of the National Energy Program has caused the Government to push cheap supplies of energy into the United States that will displace our manufacturers and our goods on the world market.
Probably the most amazing aspect of the National Energy Board decisions was the Dome Petroleum proposal to sell liquefied natural gas to the Japanese. This is an incredible situation in which a Canadian Board and the Canadian Government would allow a company like Dome to feed natural gas into the Japanese market. The Japanese market which is going soft. The Japanese are cutting back on orders of coal and natural gas. The formula by which Dome is to sell that gas to the Japanese is based on the U.S. prices. If the Government caves in to the demands of the United States to lower the price of our export gas sales, then our gas to the Japanese could easily go down. The price is already so low that when one takes into account the cost of delivering the gas from Prince Rupert, the liquefication, the transfer to Japan, and the regasification the return to Canadians will make the exercise uneconomical. In reality, we may discover that Dome will have to be bailed out from another misguided project.
There are serious concerns, even concerns expressed by the National Energy Board. I think it is time for the Cabinet to step in and put a stop to these illogical projects. We must develop a much more sound approach to the management of our economy and the development of energy as a rational, integrated part of industrial and economic development in Canada. Instead, the Government's approach has simply been to try to snatch at a goose that they thought was laying a golden egg.
These problems originally began when the Government's National Energy Program of 1980 failed miserably to develop an economic strategy for Canada. That program was patterned after the same miserable failures of past Liberal Governments' proposals to export our unprocessed resources. This is what the Liberal Government has traditionally depended upon. It has failed to develop an effective and broadly based industrial strategy with a firm foundation that is developed by Canadians and will provide employment opportunities.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources should come to the House and give us a new update to the National Energy Program. Furthermore, when we come to deal with the budget of the former Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, perhaps we will find some direction which will show that the Government has finally become aware of the real problems that confront this country and its economy. The Government should go back to square one, develop an industrial strategy that will put Canadians back to work, and that will not suffer from the ups and downs of an OPEC-managed world energy market.

My colleague, the Hon. Member for St. John's West went through the itemized performance. Since 1968 we have had one balanced budget. In the year 1969-70, there was a $493 million surplus. Since that time we have had escalations of deficit financing, to the point where our gross debt is now in the order of $135 billion to $140 billion and interest costs alone are $17 billion annually. What a tremendous imposition that is upon the productive capacity of this nation.
In order to finance the deficit we either have to borrow or print more money. We are selling out Canada and putting an imposition on future generations. The young people of this country will be faced with the burden of servicing the debt and, hopefully, paying it off some day. Quite frankly, we are spending beyond our means, and have been doing so for some time.
Massive Government borrowing on the scale of $19 billion has very serious consequences in terms of our whole economic environment. It will threaten the recovery and has the potential of fueling inflationary expectations, which can cause interest rates to rise again. There is a clear possibility that we could repeat the cycle of 1981-82 which was an economic disaster.
We face the prospect of crowding out the private sector. The Government now takes 60 per cent of the long-term capital needs generated in this country. We seem to be compounding the errors of the seventies. We are on the road to repeating the trends we followed in the seventies. When we look at the trends that are developing in terms of the amounts that all Goverments are taking as a percentage of the GNP, it is frightening. When that happens, we not only lose our economic freedom, but our political freedom is threatened as well.
Looking at the reality of the situation, we must address some of the problems facing us today. We must cut back on Government spending. We cannot reduce social assistance programs under the current crisis. Naturally, we cannot reduce the transfer payments. There are some serious structural problems in the economy. We know that we cannot reduce the deficit overnight, but we must be determined. We must develop a psychology of working toward reducing the deficit.
There are many ways in which the extravagance and excessive spending of this Government could be reduced. Let us look at this Government's record in terms of how it treats its friends, such as newly appointed Senator Pitfield. We learned the horrendous revelations of the former Minister of Energy in the sweetheart deal arranged for him. With a $25,000 investment, he has the potential of picking up a $750,000 profit, a $30,000 a year salary, plus $600 a day. That is a real sweetheart deal.
We now have the ridiculous Royal commission, which will cost Canadian taxpayers $5,000 a day, of which the chairman will receive up to $925 per day, plus expenses. On the economic side, as well, Mr. Speaker, I believe there are a number of things which have to be done, and have to be done soon. This Government is possessed with its massive intervention in the economic welfare of the country. I believe that we in this country must make a commitment toward a more market-oriented economy. I believe this would do more to restore confidence in the economic domain than anything that has occurred over the last two years. It is the reality of the world, particularly in our new industrialized nations, that we will have to recognize that the free market forces are going to have a greater play in the future.
Second, we should make it very clear to Canadians, and to people throughout the world, that we in Canada are ready and open for business, by removing the obstacles and restraints to investments, both from domestic and foreign sources. There is no question that this country needs capital to create jobs. We should become a haven for investment, rather than a country which is hostile to it. Third, as I said in my speech on the tax Bill the other day, we must simplify our complex, costly and counterproductive tax system. It is regressive. I believe we have to face the facts, Mr. Speaker, that surely we have disproven and discredited that utopian ideal that we can plan and regulate everything to perfection. Let us get on with the job. Let us unleash the entrepreneurial spirit in this country. The enterprising spirit, Mr. Speaker, will be the main engine of growth in this country.
Fourth, I am sure that we can remove duplication and reduce the level of Government take, in concert, again, with the Provinces. The former Auditor General of Canada said that he could identify some $5 million-worth of savings just in the area of reducing duplication. I thank the Hon. Member for his question. If I used the word "co-ordinate" or "manage" I left the wrong impression, because the fact of the matter is that before the National Energy Program we had a healthy oil and petrochemical industry in this country. Since the NEP, we have neither. What I am saying is that the effect of the NEP not only destroyed the oil industry as we know it, but it is also playing havoc with the petrochemical industry. What is really happening is the heavy up-front taxes-well, I will wait until the Member is prompted by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce who should have this problem resolved by now rather than sitting on it.
The fact of the matter is that because of the heavy up-front taxes on the feedstock of petrochemicals, we now find ourselves in a situation where we are non-competitive in world markets.
As to manpower policies, the federal Government is the main author of economic policy and immigration policy, so it is in a better position to determine what the needs are, what the skills are, and the number of people coming to major centres like Toronto or Montreal. So I am suggesting it has a better opportunity to provide leadership and direction than any other level of Government. It is the author of economic policy, of immigration policy. Well, I may be treading in the provincial domain, but I think there has to be better co-operation and coordination in matching the skills with the demands.
