subtopic: NATIONAL REVENUE-GARNISHEEING OF SMALL BUSINESS ACCOUNTS. (B) GOVERNMENT POLICY
NATIONAL REVENUE-GARNISHEEING OF SMALL BUSINESS ACCOUNTS. (B) GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, ten days ago I rose in my place to address a question to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan). I asked him why he would not make a recommendation to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) to impose a surtax on American potatoes, coming into the market in the lower Fraser Valley and the Greater Vancouver area. From his reply I deduced that there has been a trade-off made between the Canadian and American Governments. The Minister of Agriculture replied that we have problems in trade with the United States. I assume as a result of the problems we have with the United States that the Minister of Agriculture, maybe together with the Minister of Finance, has decided the Canadian producer in Eastern Canada cannot be put in jeopardy with the American market. Therefore, the Government is now willing to sacrifice the potato growers in the Fraser Valley of British Columbia and will let them be destroyed in order to save the eastern potato producer.
The potato product coming in from the United States is of high quality. It is produced, on an economic scale at a ratio of probably ten to one. The land costs are far below Canadian land costs and taxes are lower. Above all, labour costs are substantially lower. As a result the Canadian producer cannot produce a product competitive with the U.S. product. This means the American producer can now import and market potatoes in Canada at probably 50 per cent of the cost of

February 17, 1983
Adjournment Debate
Canadian production. Therefore, the Canadian potato farmer in the Lower Fraser Valley will not be able to exist.
I suggested to the Minister of Agriculture-that great friend of the farmer, the best Minister of Agriculture the world has ever seen-that as a result farmers will lose their farms, or they will have to divide their land and sell it to light industry in order to make a living. In other words, if farmers do not make a living from their product, they will have to go out of business.
Somehow the Minister of Agriculture does not appreciate the domino effect, the cause and effect relationship of his policies on farmers in the Fraser Valley. If farmers cannot make expenses, and if they have to go out of business-they have to make a living somehow-this means they will have their farms rezoned. But the Minister of Agriculture says zoning is a provincial problem, that is not a problem of the Minister of Agriculture. The clueless Minister of Agriculture does not see that relationship. Sooner or later these farmers will have to rezone their farms in order to gain some capital, and then invest it in some way.
The net result will be that those corporate farms in the State of Washington will capture the entire Canadian market, because there will be no Canadian suppliers. If the Minister of Agriculture is at all interested in the consumer, he ought to work for the protection of the farmer in Canada so that the consumer will not be victimized by the one sole source of supply, which will be the State of Washington. If he cares at all for the Canadian consumer, he will do everything in his power to preserve the Canadian farmer.
Under present policies he has made this trade-off and is willing to sacrifice the farmer in the Fraser Valley to preserve the farmer in eastern Canada. I do not fault him for trying to preserve the eastern farmer, but in a matter of years he will find that there are no Canadian farms in the Fraser Valley. It will all be industrial land. We will be at the mercy of the corporate farms in the United States. At that point they will be able to charge whatever price they want. They will be able to scalp the Canadian consumer because there will be no other source of supply.
I put it to you, Mr. Speaker, that this Minister of Agriculture is sacrificing, first the farmer and then the consumer, and we will pay for it in the future.

speakeroldname: Mr. Garnet M. Bloomfield (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
subtopic: NATIONAL REVENUE-GARNISHEEING OF SMALL BUSINESS ACCOUNTS. (B) GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the situation is somewhat unusual in that there has been some confusion with regard to this question and the question the Hon. Member for Surrey-White Rock-North Delta (Mr. Friesen) asked on Tuesday, February 15. This evening, I am answering the question asked last Tuesday evening, dealing with a revenue problem.
The collection policy of the Department of National Revenue, Taxation, is best described as patient but firm, becoming
increasingly more firm if the taxpayer concerned attempts to escape responsibility.
When the moneys owing are income taxes, the taxpayer is first sent an assessment notice which says that by law the taxes owing must be paid within 30 days. If the payment is not made, a reminder in the form of a resquest for payment is mailed to the taxpayer. If this second notice is not heeded, a third one is sent to inform the taxpayer that legal action may result if payment or satisfactory arrangements are not made within 15 days.
Finally, when the taxpayer has been approached three times, the Department proceeds to apply the collection powers that Parliament has given it. These are the powers of garnishee of wages or other forms of remuneration, the garnishee of bank deposits or the seizure and sale of assets. These measures may seem harsh, but the citizen who does not pay his taxes is acting contrary to the interests of fellow citizens who have paid theirs.
If the amounts owing are source deductions, the matter is even more serious. These source deductions are trust funds. The employer is withholding amounts to pay the employee's income tax, his Canada Pension Plan contributions and his unemployment insurance premiums. This is the employee's money and not the employer's, and if it were not required by law to be withheld and remitted to the Government the employer would have had to pay it to the employee.
Therefore, when the Department detects by audit or other means that an employer has failed to remit source deductions, it demands immediate payment. By that time, he would be in arrears by at least 30 days. The payroll auditor would request the money and caution the employer that failure to pay may result in legal action. I would be very surprised if any employer did not already know this.
That legal action is once again garnishment, applied, where appropriate, to accounts receivable of the business. The Department would have some knowledge of the customers of the business and would file notice with one or more of these customers that amounts they would otherwise pay to the business in default of source deductions must be paid to the Department. Of course, the garnishee notice states the amount that the business is deficient and the customer is required to divert all payments up to that amount to the Department.
I cannot see why the Hon. Member is critical of these actions. The businessman has taken trust funds and funds that were not his and has not remitted them as the law requires. The Department takes action to recover these funds in the way Parliament has provided. It is as simple as that.

subtopic: THE ADMINISTRATION-POSITION OF PRESENT MINISTERS. (B) REQUEST THAT PRIME MINISTER TAKE ACTION. (C) REQUEST FOR COMMITTEE INVESTIGATION
THE ADMINISTRATION-POSITION OF PRESENT MINISTERS. (B) REQUEST THAT PRIME MINISTER TAKE ACTION. (C) REQUEST FOR COMMITTEE INVESTIGATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the matter of Alastair Gillespie today, we witnessed in the House one of the most incredible performances ever made by a Prime Minister of our country. We are a parliamentary democracy which is based on the British tradition.
February 17, 1983

The pinnacle of our system is responsible Government. A Minister, upon joining the Government, becomes responsible for the actions within his Department, and the actions of an agency of that Department, which is under his control. If he errs in judgment in a serious way, if a major mistake is made in his Department or if one of his agencies transgresses the rules, the Minister must assume full responsibility. This, above all, is important in cases involving morality. Concerning questions of basic honesty and honourable dealings, the correct and proper course must not only be taken, but it must also be seen to have been taken.
The post-employment guidelines set forth by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) clearly stipulate as follows:
In any official dealings with the former office holders, Ministers must ensure that they do not provide grounds or the appearance of grounds for allegations of improper influence, privilege of access or preferential treatment.
Former Ministers must not:
-act for or on behalf of any person or commercial corporation in connection with a transaction to which the Government of Canada is a party and in which they had a personal and substantial involvement during the last two years of their participation in the ministry within two years of leaving office.
Neither can they lobby for or on behalf of any person or corporation within that Department for which they were responsible.
What are the facts here? We know that the former Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, Alastair Gillespie, entered into a memorandum of understanding with two Crown corporations, Petro-Canada and the Cape Breton Development Corporation, 16 months after leaving his ministry. These were the financing arrangements to set up the Scotia Coals Synfuels Project. We have seen television footage of Mr. Gillespie and the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen) announcing this project in Nova Scotia in April of 1981, six months after the signing of this particular memorandum of understanding. The press conference had national exposure and was arranged by the Press Secretary and other officials of the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources.
These events were grossly improper and constitute a massive breach of the conflict of interest guidelines. Mr. Gillespie should not have been dealing with the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources or any Crown corporation on an energy-related matter, according to the guidelines.
What is equally serious is that the current Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde), who was then Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, should not have had dealings with Mr. Gillespie, at least until after June, 1981, again according to the guidelines set down by the Prime Minister.
The Prime Minister tries to protect his Minister by saying that his Minister had no personal knowledge of the arrangement until September of 1981, when the final agreement was signed between the Government of Canada and Mr. Gillespie. However, that simply cannot be accurate. Even more important, it is not of great relevance, in my submission.
Adjournment Debate
It is clear that the Minister's Department and agencies were involved in this highly suspect arrangement for some time. The Deputy Prime Minister, the second highest elected official in the country, knew all about it, attended a press conference and must have been fully aware of the conflicts which were involved.
When a system of Cabinet and Ministerial responsibility is so grossly infringed, it is incumbent on a Minister to tender his resignation. Let us face it, Mr. Speaker, Alastair Gillespie had dickered on this deal for a long time before September, 1981, or even June of that year.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: THE ADMINISTRATION-POSITION OF PRESENT MINISTERS. (B) REQUEST THAT PRIME MINISTER TAKE ACTION. (C) REQUEST FOR COMMITTEE INVESTIGATION
speechtext: Says who?

subtopic: THE ADMINISTRATION-POSITION OF PRESENT MINISTERS. (B) REQUEST THAT PRIME MINISTER TAKE ACTION. (C) REQUEST FOR COMMITTEE INVESTIGATION
speechtext:
It was the subject of a memorandum of understanding and a press conference with the Deputy Prime Minister. When the Prime Minister suggested that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources did not even have knowledge of the matter, who was he trying to kid?
Moreover, where is the success of our system? How can he be so ignorant of the traditions upon which this institution and our democratic system are based? What of the Deputy Prime Minister? He, too, must bear responsibility here. He is second only to the Prime Minister. His face was depicted all over the television screens along with Alastair Gillespie, at least two months before Mr. Gillespie was supposed to have any dealings whatsoever with his former Department. In the words of the Prime Minister, "There is no way that Mr. Gillespie was laundered by April of 1981".
This is not a mistake. This is not an innocent omission. This was a deliberate flaunting of the guidelines conceived and set forth by the present Prime Minister. There could be no more blatant a case of public immorality. Not only has a political friend been given a special sweetheart deal, but he has also received that deal in the face of the Prime Minister's own explicit directives.
I now call upon the Prime Minister to accept his responsibilities. His Ministers have been caught contravening the conflict of interest guidelines.
If American legislators were guilty of misconduct in Abscam, as was clearly demonstrated on videotape, so was the Deputy Prime Minister caught on television announcing this particular project some time before the expiry of two years from the time Mr. Gillespie left the ministry.
If Lord Carrington in the United Kingdom was responsible, even though he had no knowledge of the items which led to the invasion of the Falklands, he as a matter of principle and honour under the parliamentary system felt obligated to tender his resignation, because something had happened in a department over which he had responsibility.
The admission of responsibility is fundamental. The Prime Minister must act immediately, swiftly, and ask for the resignation of the Minister of Finance.

February 17, 1983
Adjournment Debate

speakeroldname: Mr. David Smith (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: THE ADMINISTRATION-POSITION OF PRESENT MINISTERS. (B) REQUEST THAT PRIME MINISTER TAKE ACTION. (C) REQUEST FOR COMMITTEE INVESTIGATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since this matter was first raised in this House yesterday by the Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Nielsen) we have had a series of allegations of conflict of interest, preferential treatment, etc., raised against members of this Government, as well as a previous Minister of the Crown.
The Hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) has been accused of violating the conflict of interest guidelines during the period when he was Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. The Hon. Alastair Gillespie has been accused of violating the post-employment guidelines applied to former holders of public office. We have yet to be told what guidelines have been contravened by the Ministers of the Government of the Province of Nova Scotia, a Tory Government, I might add, as a result of that Province's participation in the agreement which has generated this tempest, which is certainly a tempest in a teapot.
I think at this time it is appropriate to review the genesis and purpose of these conflict of interest and post-employment guidelines. The first comprehensive sets of guidelines for Ministers in these areas were established by Liberal Governments under this Prime Minister, in 1973 in the case of conflict of interest guidelines, and in 1978 in the case of postemployment guidelines. The most recent guidelines were introduced by the Prime Minister in 1980.
These guidelines were established to protect the interests of the public, and the reputations of individual Ministers and office holders. In this debate, Members of the Opposition have attacked the reputations of present and past Members of the Government, with vague innuendoes that the public interest has not been well served.
I will quote the relevant section of the conflict of interest guidelines applied to Ministers:
(1)	Current and former holders of public office must ensure by their actions that the objectivity and impartiality of Government service are not cast in doubt and that the people of Canada are given no cause to believe that preferential treatment is being or will be unduly accorded to any person or organization.
(2)	Current and former holders of public office must ensure by their actions that there is no reasonable ground for belief that it is possible to have privileged access to Government personnel or services.
(3)	Current and former holders of public office must exercise care in the management of their private affairs so as not to benefit, or to appear to benefit, from the use or communication of confidential information acquired in the course of their official duties.
The Minister of Finance cannot in any way be said to have contravened the guidelines and to have given "preferential treatment" to any person or organization. His only contact with Mr. Gillespie would have been on September 25, 1981 when he signed, on behalf of Her Majesty in right of Canada, a tripartite agreement between the Government of Nova Scotia, the Scotia Coal Synfuels Project, a consortium consisting of Petro-Canada, Cape Breton Development Corp., and Nova Scotia Resources Ltd., which is provincial Crown corporation, and Mr. Gillespie and his partners, and Her Majesty in Right of Canada.

subtopic: GRAIN-TIMING OF CHANGE OF CROWSNEST PASS FREIGHT RATE-EFFECT ON EXPORTS. (B) REQUEST THAT MINISTER TABLE STUDIES
GRAIN-TIMING OF CHANGE OF CROWSNEST PASS FREIGHT RATE-EFFECT ON EXPORTS. (B) REQUEST THAT MINISTER TABLE STUDIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on February 10 I rose in the House to ask questions of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin), who speaks for the Government on matters relating to grain exports and the Canadian Wheat Board since the Senator in charge is not in this House, and of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan). I asked them both to comment on the policy moves the Government was making with regard to abandoning the Crow rate.
In my question to the Minister of Transport I tried to establish the fact that all competing countries were increasing subsidies to enable their producers to export, while at the same time we were reducing one of the few subsidies that exist for the export of grain for this country.
I then turned to the Minister of Agriculture, who has been arguing that both the East and West will benefit from the disruption of the Crow rate. I asked a very straight forward question. I asked where, in his analysis, the increased production that will occur in the East and West will take place, how it will take place, where it could be sold and, more important, at what price. I asked the Minister to table the studies that must have been made in these areas of economic research.
The Minister replied, in typical ministerial fashion, as follows:
If there are and if these are working documents that have not been made public they will be because I think that even a blind economist on a galloping horse could see that what we are saying is true.
I have no doubt that what the studies say is true, as far as it goes. It is what they do not say that is of most importance to agriculturalists and farmers in this country. They do not state the assumptions upon which the studies were based and the direction in which the research was told to move.
We know the assumptions behind some of the studies as we go through the results. For example, we know that farmers in both the East and the West are very upset with the proposals put forward and the studies that have been made public. The Minister of Transport has been quoted numerous times in the press as saying "In the East they are talking about the survival of agriculture. In the West they are talking about the survival of agriculture."
Farmers are upset because they understand the elements of agriculture more than the researchers who have been doing the work for the Ministers of Transport and Agriculture. They understand the kind of disruption to themselves, their families and communities that follow certain actions in the name of development. They understand that some of those actions in
February 17, 1983

the name of development, or progress, or whatever buzz words the planners happen to use, will be found to be obsolete, inefficient or redundant. That is the reason farmers in the East and West are worried about the survival of agriculture. They are worried about the survival of agriculture and their place in it.
The assumptions that have been made of the livestock feeding program are in accordance with those we have been told were made for the studies done by the federal Government. They showed that livestock production in Eastern Canada will continue to increase in size, and that livestock production in Western Canada will do the same. Not much time was spent on determining where that increased production would be sold.
The studies did raise some possibilties. They indicated it may be sold as a result of the increased domestic demand which may occur after the economy turns around and people can afford to eat more meat. That demand may increase because of a possible increase in population. The increased production may be exported to the United States and Japan, depending on the economies of those countries, their ability to be self sufficient and the degree of protectionism.
Those are all very nebulous factors in these studies. The only hard evidence presented is that the market in Eastern Canada, on the U.S. East Coast, the Eastern Seaboard, are as close to our producers as they are to the producers in the mid-Western United States. They point out that producers in Western Canada are as close to the California market as are the producers in the mid-Western United States.
The studies ignore, however, the question of political interference in crossing those political borders. They ignore the effective demand, because they had to make assumptions on whether those economies are going to pick up. In fact, they ignore reality. They ignore the fact that we have to compete in international markets in grain. We are geographically trapped in a region where transportation over land for up to 700 miles has to take place, compared to our competitors, who are only 100 miles to 150 miles to water transport. They ignore these realities.
Farmers are not waiting, Mr. Speaker, for a blind economist on a galloping horse to see the answers. They are simply looking for some clear-eyed politician to honestly say what sort of future is being planned for farmers of this country. They want a clear assessment of what is going to happen to them under the Government's transportation and agricultural policy. They did not get that in the documents which have been made
Adjournment Debate
public. They did not get that in the replies which we received on February 8.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jesse P. Flis (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: GRAIN-TIMING OF CHANGE OF CROWSNEST PASS FREIGHT RATE-EFFECT ON EXPORTS. (B) REQUEST THAT MINISTER TABLE STUDIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in his question of February 10, and in his remarks tonight, the Hon. Member objects to the Government's plans to reform the Crowsnest Pass freight rate on the grounds that this is the only program which allows Canadian grain farmers to remain competitive. He refers to concerns voiced by the Minister of State responsible for the Wheat Board about export grain subsidies in other countries. The key is Canada's ability to compete. In his closing remarks, the Hon. Member said the answer ignored the fact that we have to compete on the world market. I believe that is exactly what we are addressing. Our Canadian producers have to compete on the world market.
The Hon. Member, in fairness to his constituents, should look up the definition of "competitive". What is competition? Competition is not being just price competitive. In order for the Canadian producer, the Canadian farmer, to be competitive, he must, first of all, guarantee a quality product. The producer must guarantee delivery of the amount he contracted for, and he must guarantee delivery on time. In combination with all of this his or her price has to be competitive.
But even if we subsidize the farmer 100 per cent of the cost of producing transportation, if the farmer cannot meet the other terms of being competitive, that is, if he or she does not give a quality product, does not deliver the amount contracted for, does not deliver on time, then that farmer is not competitive.
Therefore, I believe, Mr. Speaker, we have to finally take a good look at what we mean by encouraging our farmers to be competitive. That is what the Western transportation initiative is all about, a better transportation system. The Government has allocated a great deal of money, almost $4 billion over four years, to this initiative, in spite of a large deficit. The Government believes it is not unreasonable to ask farmers to share in future cost increases. I spoke to farmers in the Hon. Member's constituency because I was born and raised there, and these farmers agree. When you speak to them on an individual basis, they agree they have to be realistic, they have to pay more for transportation costs. But, they say, guarantee us an efficient transportation system.
